Entertainment.title: London film festival celebrates British-Latino identity
Entertainment.text:
An event billed as London's only competitive Latino film festival is now under way for the first time in the capital.

Venues including the Barbican, the ICA, Ciné Lumière and BFI Stephen Street will screen 60 films from 27 countries until Tuesday.

There will also be workshops and performances with guests including Cuban dancer Carlos Acosta, a former principal at the Royal Ballet, Argentine actor Óscar Martínez, Cuban actor Jorge Perugorría and Oscar-winning Chilean screenwriter Gonzalo Maza.

The event was founded by Cuban actress Ketty Rodriguez who, when she moved to London, was struck by the lack of Latin representation in a city famous for its multiculturalism, film and history.

She told BBC London: "Everything here is about community, is about connection, and the idea started because I couldn't find my people, I didn't know where they were, so I decided to do this festival and it's very successful, I'm very happy."

Rodriguez says it is the first competitive Latino film festival of this size in London.

"We have received hundreds of entries from all over Latin America, and can't wait to support and showcase features, documentaries, animation, and shorts from these incredible filmmakers," she said.

Cuban dancer Javier Torres, who developed the festival idea with Rodriguez, said: "This is just the start of something great. We found a gap in the market, we found a necessity of the Latino community to come together and to give voice and narrative voices to Latin American filmmakers.

"This is a platform for diplomacy, for culture, to get together and this is what we are building here."

Alongside entries from Latin America are stories made in London for Londoners.

Victor Rios, a British-Bolivian filmmaker said the event was a chance "not just to celebrate people of Latin roots but also to celebrate British-Latino identity".

He moved to the UK at 16, and has two short films in the selection.

He said: "It's very crucial for people to understand that we are not just here passing by. We are part of society, and this festival is establishing that too.

"We're very proud to be Colombians, Bolivians, Ecuadorians, Peruvians, Chileans, but we are also British.

"So we have a place, we have a say, and we want to be heard."

The festival is backed by the BFI through National Lottery funding and by the City of London Corporation.

Entertainment.title: ‘If it’s too slick, it looks like a fashion mag’: Peter Zumthor on his £110m rammed concrete gallery
Entertainment.text:
In the early 1960s, when Peter Zumthor was a teenage apprentice in his father’s cabinet-making workshop, he designed his first cupboard. He later recalled the satisfaction of fitting the door so perfectly that it closed “with a special sucking sound”, saying his father instilled in him “the Basel pride in the well-built object”.

Six decades on, with a fleet of globally celebrated projects to his name, the 83-year-old Swiss architect is back in Basel, beaming with the same local pride. He is gazing out at his latest well-built object, which is also his first project here: a monolithic new gallery that looks chiselled from the earth, its layers of pale crumbly concrete hammered into shape, its big oak and bronze doors – their handles wrapped with leather cord – closing with that same satisfyingly expensive Swiss swoosh.

“It was an old feeling,” Zumthor tells me, describing working in his home town to build the £110m addition to the Beyeler Foundation. “I encountered craftspeople who remembered my father, who had this special knowledge of how to make things. They weren’t surprised if something had to be custom-made.”

It was quite a change from his previous building site. Fresh from the recent opening of the tortuous, two-decade-long, $724m addition to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, Zumthor is visibly relieved to be back on home turf. “The normal American architect is used to sourcing products, not looking for somebody who can make something custom-made,” he says, with a furrowed brow. “Their buildings are an assembly of products.”

Not so in Switzerland. From the pear wood handrails to the leather benches and blown glass lamps, every piece of his new gallery has been meticulously handmade. But is the sum of these bespoke parts a worthy companion to one of the country’s – if not the world’s – most beloved art museums?

Designed by Italian architect Renzo Piano, the Beyeler Foundation was hailed as a model of elegant restraint when it opened in October 1997 – the same month as Frank Gehry’s billowing Bilbao Guggenheim – praised as a sober foil to the “iconic” tendencies of the time. Sited in Riehen, just outside Basel, in the grounds of an 18th-century villa, the museum was commissioned by Ernst Beyeler, Europe’s pre-eminent modern art dealer and co-founder of Art Basel, and his wife Hildy, to house their staggering collection of Monets and Mirós, Matisses and Picassos.

A long, low, temple-like shed nestled in a garden, the foundation contains within its porphyry walls a luminous sequence of galleries, with daylight flooding through slender rooftop louvers. Piano took his hi-tech fetish and wrapped it in a luxurious stone skin, foreshadowing his bigger museums to come. But it was too small right from the day it opened. Two years later, it was extended by 12 metres and soon became the most visited art museum in the country, receiving 500,000 visitors a year. The challenge was how to extend a museum already deemed perfect by its art world patrons.

“They wanted something completely different,” says Zumthor, who was selected from a shortlist of 11 architects in 2016, after 100 were approached for their ideas. “Renzo’s building is more industrial, whereas mine is almost domestic. It is the villa that this garden was missing.”

The foundation acquired the Iselin-Weber park, a formerly private woodland adjacent to the museum campus, which now doubles its size, and where Zumthor’s gallery rises like a rocky outcrop. It is one of three new structures he has designed, along with a five-storey, timber-clad office and art-handling block, and an auditorium pavilion, conceived as an open public lounge – a particularly appealing space that can be accessed without a ticket. “Ninety per cent of the time,” says the foundation’s director, Sam Keller, “museum auditoriums are dead spaces. So we’ve turned it into a social space for people to come and hang out, read books, listen to podcasts or do some work, a real extension of the park.”

The three buildings stand as an eclectic ensemble on either side of a lane, framing a public square of sorts, where a new drinking fountain trickles into a big stone trough, as in a traditional mountain village, welcoming art pilgrims to Zumthor-ville. Stone benches built into the museum facade greet weary wanderers. “A building is something you ought to be able to lean against every now and then,” says the architect, as Maurizio Cattelan’s unnerving sculpture of a drummer boy perches perilously on the parapet overhead, intermittently hammering his drum from the rooftop.

The chance for Zumthor to finally build in Basel, a few kilometres from his birthplace, clearly brought back fond memories. In a schmaltzy new two-hour documentary by Wim Wenders called From Inside Out, the misty-eyed architect explains that this “intimate building” has “a lot to do with me growing up here”. He recounts that Jura limestone was “the stone of my youth”, describing how the village fountains and the cattle troughs “all glowed”. He wanted his own building to glow, too, so he mixed Jura stone into the concrete, and had workers tamp the dry mixture by hand, laying it at a rate of no more than 45cm a day. This is all filmed with a stirring musical backdrop. He wanted the wobbly joints between each day’s work left visible, like strata of sedimentary rock.

“I call it ‘farmer concrete’,” he says. “You see it everywhere in the mountains. They make it themselves, and they don’t vibrate the mixture, so it looks rough like this. You can see the building has a history, that hands have worked on it. It’s nice if you can see those traces. If it’s too slick, you just look like a fashion magazine.”

Zumthor’s rugged brand of “rammed concrete” has become one of his highly published trademarks (and has indeed featured in fashion magazines). There is a sense of him bringing his greatest hits to the Beyeler ensemble. He used the technique for the Bruder Klaus field chapel in rural Germany and a holiday house in Devon for Alain de Botton’s Living Architecture company. The admin block, meanwhile, bears a distinct resemblance to his atelier building in Haldenstein, also in Switzerland, its elegant oak facade (masking a concrete frame) crowned with a slender corrugated canopy.

And the pavilion draws on yet another language. It’s like a warm wooden womb that’s been dug into the landscape, surrounded by walls of glass and topped with a low upholstered acoustic ceiling, full of armchairs encouraging visitors to lounge awhile. Zumthor had to wait so long for a commission in his home town, he has turned one project into three.

The galleries themselves are quite a departure from Piano’s top-lit white cubes. After the gleaming stone exterior, the interior feels almost cave-like, Monet’s waterlilies looking muddier than ever in the ground-floor gloom. Things get brighter upstairs, with large picture windows framing pastoral views in different directions as you ascend the three floors, looking towards the Black Forest on one side and the Jura mountains on the other. Limestone terrazzo floors, lime-washed walls and pale concrete ceilings create an all-encompassing world of beige, which somehow flattens the work on show, relieved only by dark timber-lined nooks for loos and lifts.

Lozenge-shaped glass lamps (“made by the only two men in Italy who have the lung capacity to do it”, I am told) provide some ambient light, while spots highlight particular works. But you might find yourself pining for the celestial top-light of Piano’s galleries next door. Despite the architect’s protestations, it oozes the aura of a luxury boutique. As one visiting Angelino noted: “It feels like a new Skims store.”

The creamy promenade culminates in a roof terrace, with more views of pretty Swiss countryside, before visitors are shuttled down a pharaonic external stairway between the concrete walls, punched with triangular openings on one side, giving glimpses of the park and a mature ginkgo tree, around which the arms of the Y-shaped building extend. Questioned about the need for all this concrete, and its attendant carbon footprint, Zumthor is adamant. “I could not make a wooden museum,” he says. “I think it is not good for art. This kind of classical art needs more substance.”

BreakingNewsTab.title: US removes all bombers from RAF Fairford back to home stations
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford, the British military base at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter terror police.

A statement from a US department official confirmed on Sunday it had removed all of its bombers from the base back to their home stations in America.

The US did not give a reason for the withdrawal, but it follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire.

Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences near the base and subsequently released on police bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.

Whitehall sources have not disputed the decision from Washington was in response to the incident at RAF Fairford.

The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.

The UK's Ministry of Defence has not commented.

Days after the incident, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

Initially, five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF). All five were UK nationals from London.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

The sixth man, aged 25, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. Counter terror police confirmed on Saturday he had also been released on bail.

RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

Days after the incident, and before the arrest of the sixth man, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor".

Rubio did not provide further details - saying at the time he was limited on what he could say on air.

US President Donald Trump separately said he was "surprised" the five men had been released on bail.

"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' conference motion
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Israel's foreign ministry says it has banned Green Party leader Zack Polanski from entering the country, after party members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.

Israel's foreign ministry described the motion as a "clear antisemitic text" and beyond "the boundaries of legitimate political debate".

Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday. The motion, which has has divided senior party figures, defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

It has been criticised by some Jewish groups, who called the motion an "attack on the Jewish community".

"Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it," the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council said in a statement.

"Branding most British Jews and Jewish institutions 'racist' stokes anti-Jewish hatred after a year in which British Jews have been murdered attending their synagogue, stabbed in the streets, and seen their community buildings firebombed."

Israel's foreign ministry said the motion was "a stain on the history of the United Kingdom".

The party's joint deputy leaders have been at odds over the subject, with Mothin Ali backing the move, and Rachel Millward describing the wording as "problematic".

But members endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813.

"The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it says.

Discussion about the vote has dominated the conference, and exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.

Speaking after the vote, Lubna Speitan, the Green member behind the motion, argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression".

"We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions," she added.

Polanski did not vote in the debate, having left the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a by-election to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here.

Asked about the motion on Friday, Polanski said: "If your Zionism is the displacement of the Palestinian people then that is clearly racist, and I say that as a Jewish leader of a British political party."

However, he said he wanted to see the reference to a single Palestinian state changed, arguing: "I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should be deciding what the future settlement looks like."

He had also said he wanted to see the motion amended to specify that it should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.

However, both amendments favoured by Polanski were rejected by Green members.

The Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council statement referred to a "particular criticism" for Polanski "who neither spoke against the motion nor voted" but welcomed the subsequent "cross-party condemnation".

A Green spokeswoman insisted the party would protect Jewish members - and they would not be persecuted for attending synagogues which defined themselves as Zionist.

Speaking after the motion had been approved, Vivien Lichtenstein, chairwoman of Jewish Greens, told the BBC she could consider her future in the party.

Polanski has not specified whether he supports the motion passed by members, but added his name to a joint statement from the party's five MPs and deputy leaders issued after the vote.

The statement pledged to ensure the Green Party was "an anti-racist party in every way" and added that there was "no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people".

Over the course of the three-day conference, key figures in the party have expressed differing positions about the Zionism motion.

Four of the party's five MPs - Ellie Chowns, Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer, Sian Berry - had publicly opposed it, with Denyer arguing it could risk "alienating a significant proportion of Jewish people".

Chowns, as well as former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas, both spoke against the motion during the debate.

Addressing members, Lucas said: "I urge you not to support the over-simplification at the heart of this motion - a refusal to accept complexities which is leading to so many Jewish members feeling scared and unwelcome in our party."

Deputy leader Mothin Ali, who had expressed support for the motion before the vote, said it was calling for "a state that's democratic, that guarantees the rights of every single person living on that land".

He added that he was "absolutely not" calling all Jewish people who define themselves as Zionists racist.

Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

The Conservatives criticised the motion, saying it demonstrated the Green Party was "toxic to its core".

Labour chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said the vote "crosses a line" and called on Polanski to "make clear that this will not be their position moving forwards".

"It is shameful to vote against a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine and to condemn the vast majority of British Jews and Jews around the world as racist for supporting Israel's right to exist," she added.

Liberal Democrat MP Luke Taylor said the motion did not address "the rising threats" of Islamophobia and antisemitism in the UK.

He added: "This is a divisive motion that pours fuel on the fire of tensions in the UK, and will leave many British Jews feeling less safe."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Brazil election goes to run-off as right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro has won the first round of Brazil's presidential election, beating the incumbent left-wing President Lula da Silva. But he did not obtain more than 50% of the votes required to win outright.

There will be a run-off vote between these two candidates on 25 October.

Flávio Bolsonaro is the son of the former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for masterminding a failed coup attempt after losing the last election.

The election was close, with President Lula polling slightly ahead during the campaign. With 99% of the votes counted, Bolsonaro had 47.03% to Lula's 45.16% of the vote.

Bolsonaro's result exceeded expectations, meaning the second round now looks like his to lose, given some of the other presidential candidates who were knocked out in the first round were right-wing alternatives.

Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) also had the most governors, senators and federal deputies elected in the results so far, meaning the party is expected to have the most influence in Congress.

The majority of Latin America has now elected right-wing presidents, aligned to the Trump administration, and the run-off will determine whether Brazil – Latin America's largest country and economy – will follow suit or not.

After casting his ballot, Lula, 80, warned that the choice was between democracy and "barbarism".

Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people".

Lula and Bolsonaro are the two biggest names in Brazilian politics, on the left and right, and this campaign has polarised Brazil yet again: with themes of sovereignty, crime, the economy and corruption being top concerns for voters.

Lula is more popular in Brazil's poorer northeast, among low-income voters, Catholics, and women.

He is seeking a fourth term in office, after being elected in 2002, 2006 and then a later non-consecutive term in 2022. In that election, he beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% of the vote, the closest presidential election result in Brazil's history.

After that election, Bolsonaro's supporters vandalised government buildings on 8 January 2023.

Jair Bolsonaro was banned from running for re-election even before his prison sentence, but endorsed his eldest son Flávio to run in his place. Jair Bolsonaro's wife, Michelle, was elected to the Senate on Sunday.

Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to grant his father, and his supporters responsible for the January 8th riots, amnesty if elected.

He is more popular in the south, and among wealthier voters and evangelical Christians.

Bolsonaro said on Sunday he was "very happy" to have led Lula in the first-round vote, and expressed confidence that he would clinch a run-off victory in three weeks' time.

"I am very happy with the real possibility that, three weeks from now, Brazil will give a definitive answer by choosing a modern government," he said, according to AFP.

Lula admitted the outcome of the vote was "unexpected", but insisted that the race was not over.

"I admit I was convinced I would win in the first round," he said on Sunday. "The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people."

The president of Brazil's supreme electoral court said on Sunday that no evidence of international interference was found in the election.

During the campaign, President Lula made "sovereignty" a key pillar of his campaign and at times accused the United States of trying to interfere in and influence Brazil's elections. He has pledged to increase defence spending.

Earlier this year, Flávio Bolsonaro successfully lobbied the United States to designate the two biggest Brazilian gangs as terrorist organisations.

In July, Brazil refused visas for two US State Department officials who Brazil alleged were attempting to sow doubt in Brazil's electoral system, which the US called "baseless." It came after Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly told a group of foreign diplomats that Brazil's voting machines share the same origin as Venezuela's, which is false.

Last year, Donald Trump used the coup trial of Jair Bolsonaro as justification for imposing tariffs on Brazil and sanctioning some top officials and judges.

A win for Flávio Bolsonaro would likely see Brazil join the US's "Shield of Americas" coalition against narco-trafficking and align more closely with the US.

Bolsonaro has pledged though to maintain an "economically pragmatic" relationship with China, which has overtaken the US as Brazil's biggest trading partner and is a crucial customer for Brazil's soy and beef exports.

Lula has criticised the US terrorist designation of Brazilian gangs but has launched various reforms to tackle the financial networks of organised crime networks, improve homicide investigations, and invest in prisons.

The economy has been central to this campaign, too: the country has high levels of personal debt and slowing growth.

Lula has defined his legacy through a series of social welfare programmes, mostly notably Bolsa Família, that pays families to ensure children stay in education and receive healthcare such as vaccines, as well as building more universities. The programmes have been credited with lifting millions of Brazilians out of poverty.

He has backed more investment in data centres and rare earth minerals, which Brazil is rich in, with strong state involvement to ensure that Brazil benefits.

He has also backed oil drilling exploration near the mouth of the Amazon River, which has proved controversial with environmentalists, but he has a record of tightening environmental protections and reducing the rate of deforestation in the Amazon. Deforestation increased significantly under Jair Bolsonaro's presidency.

Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged a public debt ceiling and government spending cuts, a revision of social welfare, and to bolster the critical minerals sector.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Protesters scuffle with police as migrants brought ashore on south coast
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Around 150 anti-migrant demonstrators gathered in a south coast town to stop a group of migrants, who had crossed the English Channel in a small boat, being brought ashore by the RNLI.

Some flares were set off and there were a few scuffles with police during the stand-off at a marina in Gosport, Hampshire, that lasted into the early hours of Monday morning.

The Home Office said 149 migrants picked up in a mid-Channel rescue operation by the RNLI alongside a French vessel.

They were taken by coach to a processing centre in Kent. It is the second known landing of large numbers of migrants this far west along the south coast in recent years.

A police cordon was in place on Haslar Road in Gosport, where the atmosphere at the protest mostly remained peaceful.

Some protesters stopped police vans from advancing by standing in front of them and chanting "shame on you" and "deport the lot".

Hampshire Police said it deployed officers to "support our partners in the event of an emergency at sea". The force imposed conditions under the Public Order Act as well as powers prohibiting the wearing of face coverings.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border."

They added it was "vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival".

The migrant dinghy appeared to have set off from near Utah Beach in Normandy on Sunday morning, according to ship tracking data.

It is the third crossing in a month. So far this year 19,451 people are recorded as having crossed the Channel in small boats.

That number is 43% lower than this time last year and 23% below the figure at this stage in 2024.

Last month, more than 100 migrants landed at Eastney in Portsmouth, leading to more scuffles between police and demonstrators.

The 51 migrants were were ultimately taken to Dover by sea.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Andrew Griffith to unveil Tory plans to cut taxes and regulations
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith is to outline his plans for the UK economy, including hopes to cut taxes, red tape and house-building costs.

Griffith and his colleagues will use day two of the party's conference in Birmingham to also explain how they would want to reduce food costs, support Heathrow Airport expansion and abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency.

Another prospective policy is replacing agreements designed to compel developers to fund community projects and services in areas they want to build.

Griffith will describe his approach as the "most ambitious deregulation project in a generation". Reform UK suggested the Tories were "copying our policies".

Griffith's speech comes after Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch published a 100-page document, external explaining her guiding principles and how her party would act should it return to government by winning the next general election.

Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again.

The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government, including on the economy, between 2010 and 2024.

Griffith is expected to say: "No-one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation."

He will accuse Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to pursue a "socialist fever dream of the 1970s", adding the Tories want to deliver "cheaper homes, lower taxes, and less red tape".

Chancellor John Healey last week said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space".

During a series of speeches on Monday, Conservative shadow ministers will continue to make their case and provide more details of their proposals.

This will include ditching environmental and energy efficiency regulations, including the future homes standard.

The Tories believe their changes could cut the cost of delivering a new home by up to £50,000, which in turn they expect could save money for buyers.

A single levy for developers would be implemented in place of section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy, which fund projects in the community when building plans are progressed.

The Conservatives argue this new charge would remove delays and improve how the funds are spent to the benefit of residents.

The party has been critical of the roles of Natural England and the Environment Agency in relation to house building and flood prevention work respectively, and wants to abolish both. Their functions would be looked after by the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).

The Extended Packaging Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires firms to cover the cost of collecting, recycling and disposing of packaging it produces, would also be scrapped by the Conservatives.

The party believes this would help lift a "burden" from businesses and in turn could cut the cost of the weekly shop.

On Heathrow, Griffith is expected to say the next Conservative government would do "whatever it takes to end the delays and boost capacity by backing the third runway".

Plans for expansion were scrapped by the Tory-led coalition government in 2010.

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves championed the runway to boost the economy after Labour won power, although Burnham has refused to say whether he backs the project since becoming prime minister.

Burnham has described it as "principally... a matter for London and Londoners".

Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the Conservatives have "cemented their position as a pointless anti-growth anti-business party" by rejecting closer ties with Europe.

She added: "No-one can take anything the Conservatives say on the economy seriously given their litany of fantasy-land financial pledges."

Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick accused the Conservatives of "once again copying our policies".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Potty-training scheme to expand to more parts of England after city's success
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The number of children who were toilet-trained before starting school this year has increased significantly in a city where parents were given potty training guides with their first school offers.

York was the subject of the city-wide pilot, which also put on workshops for parents and offered special training for early years staff.

Twenty local authorities across England are now signed up to launch similar schemes to tackle the number of pupils starting school without being fully toilet-trained.

The government said the pilot's results were "encouraging", and confirmed they were committed to 75% of pupils reaching a good level of development at the end of their first year in school by 2028.

Since April this year, parents across York have been targeted via GP surgeries, pharmacies, family hubs, schools and nurseries with information and offers of support on how to potty-train their child ahead of starting school.

Potty training guides were sent out to all families across York who had a child starting reception in September - with the aim that all children could use the toilet independently by the time they started school, except those with medical issues or special educational needs.

The results from all 55 mainstream primary schools across the city, shared exclusively with BBC News, suggested there had been a 43% drop since last year in the number of children who were not fully toilet-trained when they started school.

Across York last September, 148 out of 1,364 reception pupils (11%) were recorded as not being toilet-trained when they started school. This year, that fell to 85 reception pupils out of 1,374 (6%).

Parents Natalie and Lucy, who both have daughters starting reception next year, have welcomed the extra support on offer.

Lucy said she had noticed the drop-in sessions on potty training in her local children's centre and thought it was a "really good idea".

"I think it's really important that children are more prepared for that aspect of starting school," she said.

Natalie said getting her daughter Freya potty-trained in time for school has been a priority, but feels there is a lot of pressure on parents to do so.

"I think going to school is hard enough for children," she said.

"But for me it was really important that she's confident enough to use toilets, to be independent, to be able to go without relying on the help of teachers perhaps in an environment where they've already got lots of children to look after."

Natalie said the popularity of disposable nappies might be a reason why parents often wait longer to potty train.

"When I was little, we still had the terry towelling nappies and they had to be washed and hung on the line. So I think with disposable nappies it's easier," she said.

York councillor Bob Webb said the impact of the scheme had been "so positive" for both schools and families.

But he acknowledged a potential "gap in support" for parents between seeing health visitors with their toddler, and the child later arriving at school.

He said the key to the scheme's success was collaboration across health visitors, schools and other community settings, but that there was "always more that could be done at an earlier age".

Twenty local authorities across England have now committed to adopt York's model, developed by Kindred Squared, and use it to encourage earlier potty-training in their areas.

North Lincolnshire

London Borough of Redbridge

London Borough of Hounslow

Cheshire West and Chester

Just over two-thirds of children in England (68.3%) leave reception class with a good level of development - a key measure of school readiness which includes things like communication skills, as well as physical, social and emotional development - according to the latest government stats, external.

That means they were assessed by teachers on being able to complete tasks like going to the toilet and paying attention in class.

The government has said it is still committed to increasing that proportion to 75% by 2028.

Early Education Minister Paul Waugh said it was "encouraging to see this pilot helping more children develop the confidence and independence they need before starting school", stressing the importance of parents taking early steps towards toilet training.

In York, Mould said she hopes next year's parents will take on potty-training even earlier.

"Ideally we'd be at the point where [children] don't need that support when they get here, because they've already been trained by the time they get to us."

BreakingNewsTab.title: France to close up to 500 schools on Monday over student protests
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday.

Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Édouard Geffray said.

He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests.

Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.

High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.

On Friday, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests.

The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons".

"There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Édouard Geffray claimed.

"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before".

On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Girl, 12, fatally shot in US during 'dispute over parking space'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A 12-year-old girl was killed in Baltimore over the weekend during an apparent disagreement over a parking space, police in the US city said.

The girl was caught in the crossfire of bullets between two men who police said were allegedly fighting over a parking space in a park where children were playing American football.

In addition to the young girl, a woman was also found with gunshot wounds when police arrived on the scene. Two men also visited area hospitals for injuries believed to be related to the shooting, police said.

Police are now searching for at least two suspects, Baltimore Police Commissioner Richard Worley said at a news conference. No arrests have been made.

"What we know is there was some type of argument between two cowards," Worley said. "They both opened fire on each other. In the crossfire, a 12-year-old little girl, who was probably down there watching football, was shot and killed."

Worley said the girl, who police have not named, was not a target of the shooting.

The girl was pronounced dead in hospital. The other three individuals who were injured have non-life-threatening injuries, Worley said.

The incident happened after 18:00 EDT (23:00 BST) on Saturday.

Authorities are still investigating the shooting and have asked any witnesses to bring information to police.

It remains unclear how many shots were fired, Worley said.

"Two grown men got into an argument, and now a 12-year-old is gone," Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott said at the news conference.

"We never should have to say something like that. What happened out here today is one of the most disgusting things I've ever seen in my life."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Yemen government announces major operation to retake Houthi territory
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The head of Yemen's internationally recognised government has announced it will wage an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis.

It follows an exchange of strikes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition in recent days.

The Iran-backed group said it had struck sites belonging to Saudi national oil company Aramco, in response to what it described as 50 Saudi-led coalition strikes in 12 hours. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment.

The Yemeni government's fierce statement was expected after the Houthis' offensive last month, which saw them seize control of the country's coastline, including the vital shipping lane of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

On Sunday, Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address: "Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory."

Yemen's capital, Sanaa, which has been held by the Houthis for more than a decade, has come under sustained attack as government forces try to weaken the group's military capabilities.

Attacks on the Houthis have also spread across Yemen, including to the Saada region, the group's northern heartland.

But security sources say the Iran-backed Houthis have continued to make gains.

The frontline in Yemen remains focused around the key city of Taiz, which is still controlled by the internationally recognised government.

On Sunday, the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government, AFP news agency reports.

Citing three Yemeni military sources, AFP also reports that the Houthis now control the area and supply route, effectively encircling Taiz.

"They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it," Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the Chatham House think tank, told AFP.

Al-Alimi was unlikely to have made the fierce announcement without the green light from Saudi Arabia, which remains the key backer of his government.

Saudi Arabia has been under constant attack as the Houthis try to target the country's economic lifeblood - oil.

On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east.

"Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites."

It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories".

But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis.

In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday.

On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west.

BreakingNewsTab.title: I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and a 100 page statement on her guiding principles., external

"I believe in common sense, people working hard and being rewarded for that effort," she told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.

She added that welfare should be a "safety net, not a lifestyle".

The Tory leader is trying to ensure her party stands out in a crowded political field. The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in the opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than that of her party, has characterised Reform leader Nigel Farage as a "grumpy grandpa" and she told Laura Kuenssberg that Labour leader Andy Burnham is "the cheesy uncle who does all the dad jokes".

She described herself as a "no-nonsense mum".

Asked if her plan for benefit cuts and a massive increase in prison places was a return to the "nasty party" of the past, she said: "It's the common sense party. That's what we're doing.

"And, quite frankly, if we were doing so well the old way, then why did we have such a terrible issue in 2024?"

In her essay The Right Way - a deliberate echo of an essay written by Margaret Thatcher in 1976, external entitled The Right Approach - Badenoch says the last Conservative government failed because it did not know what it stood for.

Despite the party's rhetoric during its 14 years in power, she said: "We did little to reverse the structural changes Labour had made which took the country in the wrong direction.

"The result was that the state grew by stealth."

The essay says the "next Conservative government will have one central principle: business, not government, creates growth".

The Tories would achieve growth through tax cuts, cutting red tape and reducing the size of the civil service back to pre-pandemic levels, the essay says.

And it adds: "What is really missing from politics and government today is people prepared to say no.

"Political parties now need to recruit those who have the stomach to say no to good causes when the resources simply are not there to do everything."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Christa Pike's prognosis still unclear after failed execution, lawyer says
BreakingNewsTab.text:
US murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear following her failed execution, her lawyer has said on Sunday.

Speaking to CNN on Sunday morning, Pike's lawyer Stephen Ferrell said doctors were still trying to clear two doses of pentobarbital from her body.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death following her conviction for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.

She survived two execution attempts on Wednesday, and was transferred to a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee.

Ferrell said: "She's still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill, we really don't know the prognosis yet, and may not know for several days."

He didn't believe she had regained consciousness at any point, adding that he has been receiving updates through her medical power of attorney rather than consulting directly with doctors.

He has not been in to see her. "She is guarded. I'm not sure who may have seen her," he said.

Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. But Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said he would resign on Saturday.

"If she recovers - she may not fully recover - and there may be issues about her competence. I mean, we just don't know any of this," Ferrell said. "We have had no discussions about this. The Tennessee attorney general's office so far has not given us any indications of what their intentions will be."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Major bridges in Kyiv have been hit by Russian drone strikes for four consecutive days, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital.

Two people were injured when the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge was struck on Sunday morning for the second day in a row, while the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times earlier in the week.

The latest attack came as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made a surprise visit to Kyiv in a show of support against Russia's continuing full-scale invasion.

Russia's military said it would be intensifying strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions. It earlier said it had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were injured in the latest Russian attack. He earlier said that the Pivnichnyi Bridge's roadway was hit.

Kyiv's eight bridges across the wide Dnipro River link the western (right) and eastern (left) parts, and many of the capital's estimated three million residents rely heavily on the metro lines and trains to travel across the city.

Some 500,000 vehicles use the bridges every day.

The two struck bridges are still standing - but the damage and restrictions to traffic and public transport have caused gridlock in parts of the capital at times.

"To get from the left bank to the right one and back - it's just hell," Kyiv resident Roman told the BBC on Sunday.

Large numbers of commuters cross the river, especially on weekdays. Repair teams are working to fix the damage and officials say they are planning temporary pontoon bridges, ferry services and even a tunnel under the river to keep Kyiv connected.

Klitschko also said a separate Russian drone strike had damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenksy said on Sunday morning Russian drones had also attacked a warehouse in the north-eastern region of Sumy, killing one person.

Meanwhile, in the central city of Dnipro, six people were injured after a communications facility was struck, he said.

Ukraine's Air Force said that overnight Russia had launched 135 drones, including 52 jet-powered ones. It said that 125 projectiles had been shot down.

As emergency services responded to the incidents, Germany's Merz met Zelenksy in Kyiv. They laid wreaths to Ukrainian soldiers who have been killed in the war.

Merz reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine, writing on X: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.

"Germany's security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well."

Zelensky later said that a new aid package worth more than €1.3bn (£1.1bn; $1.5bn) had been agreed with Germany.

"These are weapons that will help [us] right now, as well as support for our energy sector ahead of winter," he said.

As Merz was visiting Ukraine's Academy of Sciences building badly damaged in a Russian drone attack earlier this week, fresh air alert sirens were heard across the city. Two people were killed in that drone attack.

Since Merz became chancellor in May 2025, Germany has become the single largest donor to Ukraine.

He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us."

Zelensky said there would be "important agreements" made between Ukraine and Germany.

The Ukrainian president has made repeated appeals for Western allies to provide more military support to the country, including supplying advanced interceptors that can shoot down new jet-powered Russian drones and also ballistic missiles.

The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier this week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had earlier said his military was carrying out retaliatory attacks following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities, despite the fact that it was the Kremlin that had first launched such attacks.

Putin began a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

The Russian foreign ministry on Saturday repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.

Responding to the warning, EU ambassador Katarína Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!"

German ambassador to Ukraine, Boris Ruge, reacted to Mathernova's post with: "Amen - we're staying".

FinanceTab.title: The job interview question you don't have to answer
FinanceTab.text:
Prepare all you like, but there is often still one job interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable.

While employers in the UK are within their rights to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, applicants are not obliged to tell them.

Recruiters have been encouraged to stop posing questions about salary history and, in the EU, new rules will prevent them doing so.

But in the UK, there is still a chance of it coming up, so how best should you answer?

When interviewing or deciding on new staff, employers must not discriminate against an applicant based on so-called protected characteristics, including age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation.

Sometimes it feels like interviewers, and interviewees, tip-toe around the subject of money.

But Louise Rudd, a senior adviser at the workplace advice and conciliation service Acas, says there are no regulations that prevent employers from asking interviewees about their current salary, or their salary expectations.

She says employers, if they do want to know, should ask each applicant the same questions to ensure they are treated fairly.

A few years ago, a campaign was launched urging employers to stop asking new recruits how much they were paid in their previous jobs. It had its own hashtag - #EndSalaryHistory.

The Fawcett Society, which campaigns for women and gender equality, said that asking the question risked maintaining historic unfair differences in pay due to gender, race and disability inequality.

Rather than offering a salary based on skills, experience and performance, it meant employers rewarded an individual's perceived worth and negotiating skills instead, the society said.

When you're going for a new job, you can reveal your current salary if you are happy to.

Some people asked by BBC News out and about in London suggested they would reply with an inflated salary - so they get paid more in the next job. However, the risks of lying in an interview can far outweigh the possible reward.

There are no requirements for you to disclose your salary if you don't want to.

Rudd says some people might prefer to give their salary expectations, or outline their understanding of the salary range for the role.

Recruitment firms often say applicants could instead focus on their skills and experience, so those are used as a measure of what they should be paid, not their salary history.

Shazia Ejaz, director of campaigns at the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, says jobseekers should approach questions about pay with "realism but also confidence".

"Candidates can focus on showcasing the value they bring, the benefits that matter most to them and to go to the interview knowing the market rate for the role," she says.

"Jobseekers who have done their homework on salaries and can explain the contribution they will make are in the strongest position to secure the right package."

FinanceTab.title: Trade: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
FinanceTab.text:
Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a batter economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China.

Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%.

Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked.

Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300mn in 2020 to $100mn this year, while exports rose from around $129mn to $200mn in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market.

The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world.

Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year.

"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC.

More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period.

"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI).

If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava.

On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address, external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues".

But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC.

That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods.

To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones.

"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava.

It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment.

Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank.

"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production.

Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends.

China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output.

Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year.

A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava.

FinanceTab.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
FinanceTab.text:
The G7 has announced 100 million barrels of oil and diesel will be released to ease supply concerns that have caused prices to skyrocket.

It includes a "substantial release" of diesel within 20 days, with discussions around "additional diesel releases as necessary", G7 leaders said in a statement.

The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would begin immediately and would last for four months.

Under the measures, which come after US President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports, there will not be any "export restrictions on energy and energy products" between G7 members.

The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.

Donald Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market. That would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.

On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."

His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.

Speaking later at the White House, Trump said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".

Referring to the decision by the G7 to release fuel from reserves, he added that "what Europe did was a great thing."

"Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution - and so are we," he said.

"And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do."

Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban early last week, and was still considering it on Thursday, as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies.

Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.

Following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the co-ordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).

The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".

Macron said the co-ordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".

In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a co-ordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."

It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.

The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.

Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.

European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.

The G7 leaders said they will also co-ordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.

FinanceTab.title: Suppliers pile pressure on government over energy bills
FinanceTab.text:
The government should take immediate action to help those struggling with energy bills this winter, the suppliers' trade body has said.

Energy UK said domestic gas prices, which rose on Thursday, and forecasts of steep rises in January meant inaction would lead to a longer-term, more costly and deeper crisis.

Figures revealed by the BBC earlier this week showed forecasters predicting a 16% rise in domestic energy prices in the new year for 20 million households on variable tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the government was considering any measure that took the pressure off.

Households in England, Scotland and Wales on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity, were hit with a 4% price increase at the start of October.

That is the equivalent of about £60 per year - or £5 per month - taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.

But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Consultancy Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggested the same typical annual bill would rise to £1,999.

Energy UK said it accepted the government had already provided some support. VAT on electricity bills was cut on Thursday, and some levies were cancelled or shifted into taxation earlier this year.

But the trade body said these savings had been wiped out by high wholesale prices, paid by suppliers, that were the result in part of international events - namely conflict in the Middle East and the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

It said bills were soaring as they had in 2022 when they were driven up by the impact of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

"We cannot afford to wait for the same scale of crisis before acting again. We must heed the lessons from that time," said Dhara Vyas, chief executive of Energy UK.

She said that the urgent intervention needed was highlighted by growing levels of customer debt, the cost of which now added an average of £67 a year to everyone's bills.

FinanceTab.title: UK diesel prices top £2 a litre for first time, RAC says
FinanceTab.text:
The average price of diesel has risen above £2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring group.

Diesel has now hit an average of 200.01p a litre, the RAC said, and petrol prices are also still rising, reaching 174.71p a litre on average.

The motoring group said price rises were "showing no signs of slowing, heaping more misery onto motorists".

Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and refined products from the region, causing prices to surge worldwide.

Ukrainian attacks on Russian refiners have further constrained supplies of diesel on the world market. China has also restricted exports of refined fuels.

Separately on Friday, G7 nations agreed at an urgent meeting to release 100 million barrels of oil to head off further price increases.

The G7 also agreed member countries would not impose export restrictions on each other, after US President Donald Trump threatened to ban shipments of American diesel overseas.

The move would have pushed up global prices of the fuel, but helped ease pressure on US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections.

RAC policy head Simon Williams said £2 was a "price threshold no one wanted to cross".

"This will be very challenging for households and companies that drive a lot of miles, from commuters, haulage and delivery firms, businesses with large fleets all the way through to sole traders," he added.

UK businesses and consumers already feel like they are bearing the brunt of higher prices, with many saying it has made their lives increasingly difficult.

Even people who do not drive a diesel vehicle themselves face a knock-on effect from rising delivery costs or the higher cost of producing food.

Mark Means, who has farmed in Norfolk for over 50 years, said he was "frightened to death" by the rising costs of diesel.

He has spent £50,000 on new diesel tanks to try to ensure he has enough supply to harvest and plants crops, but the rising price is cutting into his margins.

"It feels like it's an assault," he said.

Steven Tompkins in Leicester said rising fuel prices mean driving instructors like him are having to increase their prices.

"When you've got kids who are working part time, they're on a tight budget and we're telling them that the prices are going to have to go up because of the fuel, it's hurting," he said.

FinanceTab.title: US jobs market sees sharp slowdown ahead of midterm elections
FinanceTab.text:
The US jobs market saw a sharp slowdown in September, with employers adding just 29,000 jobs in the final update before the midterm elections.

Headcounts were little changed in major sectors from tech to retail as hiring fell significantly from August, according to figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

Meanwhile, the unemployment rate rose slightly from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September.

The figures signal a cooling US economy, which experts said reduced the likelihood of a series of further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.

The 29,000 jobs created in September was down from a figure of 133,000 in August, according to revised BLS figures for the month.

But George Brown, senior economist at Schroders, said while job gains have been a “rollercoaster“ this year, a single soft report is unlikely to point to a lasting collapse.

And Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics, said the lower figure was “not disastrous“, adding that a drop in government roles and temporary visa policy changes weighed on overall growth.

Jeffery Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial, added that the data showed tension between “goods producing sectors that support the AI boom” and service industries feeling the effect of changes brought about by the tech.

“Given the overall softness of the labour market, the likelihood of two Fed hikes is going lower,” he said.

The BLS report stands in sharp contrast to President Donald Trump's insistence that America's economy is booming and it is the "hottest" nation in the world.

The disconnect is likely to present significant challenges as the president and his fellow Republicans hit the the campaign trail with just a month to go before the midterm congressional elections.

According to an AP/NORC poll released on Thursday, just 17% of Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.

Both are new lows for Trump, surpassing the lowest mark for Democrat Joe Biden during his presidential term.

There have been some indications that the president understands that his views of the American economy are out of step with those of most Americans.

"I've done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing," he said at a White House event earlier this week.

FinanceTab.title: Why Gen Z are opting out of workplace pensions
FinanceTab.text:
Until early September, Hassan Nassar, 26, was saving around £430 every month into his NHS workplace pension.

But the trainee GP, who works in the West Midlands, says he was "really cash strapped" and decided to stop putting money aside for around "six to 12 months".

He needs the money to help take care of a sick family member, save for his first home and cover rent and student loan repayments.

But he's aware there is a cost to opting out, estimating he could lose between "£5,000 and £10,000" in future retirement income due to the decades of compound interest he will miss out on by not saving now.

"People will say, you're silly, look at what you'll be missing out in the future," he tells the BBC. "But I need to look at what I'd be losing now if I didn't opt out."

All employees will be automatically enrolled, external in a workplace pension if they are aged 22 or above and earn over £10,000, although there are exceptions.

A percentage is taken directly from the worker's pay - usually around 5% - with tax relief added on top, and the employer must also pay a minimum contribution on top.

But a growing number of Gen Z and millennials are opting out of these schemes due to cost-of-living pressures and the government has warned they could be on track for lower private pension incomes than people retiring today.

That is a problem, because while most people in the UK will eventually get a state pension, it only provides a minimum level of retirement income and many will rely on a private pension to supplement it.

Hassan says he was paying 10.7% of his gross earnings each month into his workplace pension, while the NHS contributed a substantial amount on top.

But unlike some employers, the NHS doesn't allow staff to reduce their contributions when times are hard.

Overall, however, he is confident he will have enough to retire on at the end of his "30-40" year career and is determined to opt back in to his pension as soon as he can.

According to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), around 22.6 million people, or 90% of those who are eligible for "automatic enrolment" pensions, are paying into one, while about 2.5 million are not.

However, Pensions Minister Torsten Bell told the BBC that "a rising number of young workers aren't saving, and overall there is a danger tomorrow's retirees are on track for lower private pension incomes than today's".

Evie, 22, from Cornwall, says she opted out of entering the workplace pension at the London events company she works for.

A recent drama school graduate, she says she would have struggled to cover her outgoings, including food, travel and the £800 she pays in rent.

Evie is conscious about missing out on saving for retirement, but there are other things she needs money for that make it impractical right now.

"How can I save for a house, how can I save for a car and afford my outgoings? I don't want to just work day in, day out to live, I want to work to have a life."

And she thinks she missed out on saving about £5,000 into her pension pot.

She's in a better place financially now, but recently became self-employed and is no longer part of a private pension scheme, something she hopes to change.

"I would like to feel my pension is secure, and I don't feel like that. I worry I'm not going to be able to live comfortably at the age of retirement."
