TechnologyTab.title: Trump unveils 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy
TechnologyTab.text:
US President Donald Trump says he has created a new taskforce focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday.

It comes after the president signed an executive order on 29 September to rename AI as Super Intelligence, after previously saying the word artificial made it sound "fake".

Trump also said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" pact.

"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote.

Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research, Engineering Emil Michael and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will also be part of the taskforce.

It will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

The taskforce's chief, Clayton, took office as the US national intelligence director in August after Trump's original choice, Bill Pulte, was rejected by lawmakers.

On AI, Clayton has previously said: "When something's both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."

Clayton previously served as US attorney for the Southern District of New York, overseeing several prominent cases, including the drug trafficking case against former Venezuelan President Nicholas Maduro.

The announcement of the taskforce follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.

In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public.

"The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.

Trump has dismissed calls for stronger oversight and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves.

The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google.

TechnologyTab.title: Bahrain GP in Malaysia: Lewis Hamilton bemused after F1 'Lego race'
TechnologyTab.text:
Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton likened the effects of a software bug that affected multiple cars before the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to a "Lego race".

The problem led to several cars, including those of the two multiple world champions who were sharing the front row of the grid, not working in the wet conditions that preceded the race.

A tropical downpour delayed attempts to get the grand prix under way for the best part of an hour. And when the cars set off on formation laps behind a safety car to test the conditions, audiences were treated to the bizarre sight of many of them struggling to move.

A bug in the software that mandates how the engines' electrical power can be used in wet conditions had been triggered by a combination of low engine speeds, low grip and specific aspects of the circuit layout.

Verstappen, who went on to take a dominant win that was his first victory of the year, said: "These engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented.

"I triggered [the problem] first and then I looked in my mirror, I was like, 'Wait, are they waiting for me or what's going [on]...?' It was like the Lego race."

Verstappen was referring to a show run in battery-powered Lego F1 cars that was held before the British Grand Prix in July.

Hamilton, sitting beside Verstappen in the post-race news conference after finishing third, interjected to say: "Yeah, we had the same speed. I had to stop on track and stop the car and engine and restart it. I've never done that before."

Verstappen added: "It was insane. Like, it's the Lego power. At some point we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn't understand what was going on.

"Then we did a lap and then I see eight other cars crawling still, and I saw you (Hamilton) by yourself crawling. That's not what you want, right, for the sport."

Mercedes driver George Russell, who retired from the race with an engine failure, said: "It didn't feel very F1."

Nikolas Tombazis, the single-seater director for governing body the FIA said there would be a full investigation.

The issue arose, he added, because, while the software had been tested, it had not been tested in these specific conditions. Largely because there has been so little running in the wet this year.

"Cars are complicated," Tombazis said. "We would all like it to be simpler, but when you have electrical energy and combustion energy all working together, and obviously when you want to ensure that there's sporting fairness between the teams, that is complicated.

"We haven't done a full debrief of the situation and see how we can avoid such an issue. Every race, we have a long debrief afterwards, where we identify criticalities.

"Obviously, that was a major criticality, and we need to make sure we avoid it. Can I guarantee it will never happen again? This specific problem, yes. A problem, no, but we will do our best to avoid it, of course."

This is far from the first issue created by the huge complexity of the latest hybrid engines introduced this year, with their near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power.

Because the engines are fundamentally energy starved, and so cannot deploy their full combined power output at all times, a series of complexities were added into the management of the engines to try to sticking-plaster solutions.

Many of these led to the counter-intuitive driving about which many of the sport's stars have been complaining all season - and more changes have been added since.

Off-track conversation has been dominated by this all year, and rules are changing for next year to alter the energy split to try to ameliorate the issue.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "What happened at the start obviously is not ideal in terms of presentation of the sport.

"But at the same time it is the first year of new regulations, quite complex from a regulatory point of view, and it was also the first time we started in such conditions.

"So we have to concede that F1 has done an excellent job in making some new regulations that came with some question marks from a power-unit behaviour point of view when it came to racing for instance.

"We have to acknowledge there has been really good work to make the show and racing work, and if there are some glitches occasionally, we have to accept they are glitches for everyone, be supportive and make sure it doesn't happen again."

The problem had a secondary consequence - the field order was jumbled up, and one reading of the rules could have meant the grid order should change for any restart.

But while the FIA's software engineers were rewriting the code as fast as possible, it was determined that, as this situation had never occurred before, and as the problem was out of any competitor's control, the most appropriate order was to revert to the original grid.

Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: "If you think of the millions of people watching around the world, they tune in for the start and suddenly the cars are all in a jumbled up order because of something that happened 40 minutes earlier and it was behind a safety car on a formation lap. That would have been a much harder thing to explain than resetting and then going from where we did."

"Amazing" was the word Verstappen chose to describe his and Red Bull's first win of the 2026 season at a chaotic, bizarre and, in some ways, unprecedented race.

It would be wrong to say the victory was a complete surprise, as it came after three consecutive podium finishes in which the four-time champion appeared to be edging closer and closer to such an achievement.

But it certainly adds a fresh twist to a season of fluctuating fortunes at the front, in which the only real constant has been Kimi Antonelli, as the championship heads into its final stretch.

It was Verstappen's 72nd victory and it came in a manner entirely familiar to those who have followed his career - but entirely unfamiliar to this season.

The Dutchman was the man all weekend at Sepang, where Verstappen also won the last time the track held a race in 2017. As early as Friday afternoon his rivals were all saying he was going to be difficult to beat.

He duly delivered a dominant win, which barely looked in doubt even through the chaos of a delayed start, software glitches caused by a bug in the mandated FIA engine settings that wreaked havoc for him and several other drivers on a formation lap, losing the lead to the two Mercedes off the line and a late safety car period.

What was remarkable about that, though, is that until Malaysia not once so far this season had Verstappen had been in this position.

Red Bull started this year in a bit of a state.

The fourth fastest car among the big four teams, it was debatable at times in the early races whether their car was even better than that of their junior team, Racing Bulls.

All year, Verstappen has been battling an inconsistent handling balance and there was doubt for some time as to whether he would even stay at Red Bull beyond this year.

Although contracted until the end of 2028, it was widely known there were performance-related clauses in his contract that allowed him to leave, and McLaren courted him in the summer.

In the end, though. Verstappen decided to stay, saying he liked the environment at Red Bull, he had faith they would return to the front, and he did not mind a bit of extra work helping them do it.

Those sentiments were expressed in an interview at the Italian Grand Prix a month ago. He finished third that weekend, but even that recently there was no indication a performance such as this was in the offing.

But a trickle of upgrades in the past few races finally all came together with the introduction of a new floor in Baku, the weekend before Malaysia.

There, awkward circumstances in qualifying left him eighth on the grid when by merit he would have been on the front row. But a late safety car closed up the field, and he spent the final stint right on the gearbox of George Russell's leading Mercedes, and lost out on the win by less than 0.2secs.

Malaysia proved that promise was more than a flash in the pan.

"We had a very complicated and tough start to the year with all sorts of problems and just not being competitive enough,' Verstappen said on Sunday.

"But throughout the year, the team has been working very hard to understand our issues and bring good performance upgrades to the car and make it more driveable.

"Step by step, we've been getting closer and closer, and today, and of course especially this whole weekend, we've been really in good form. So, yeah, it's amazing."

There are six or seven races remaining, depending on whether F1 gets the security reassurances it needs to give it the final confidence to commit to the end of the season grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi in the context of the war in the Middle East.

On this basis, Verstappen could well be a factor in all of them.

If the championship battle had any jeopardy remaining in it, that would certainly up the ante. But Russell's retirement from third place with an engine failure with five laps to go in Malaysia has pretty much eradicated that.

Antonelli's second place and Russell's retirement extended the Italian's lead to 84 points. With either 158 or 183 remaining in total, depending on how the season ends, that size of lead means only some kind of miraculous turn of events could turn the tide back in Russell's favour.

He said: "I don't need to say I think it's gone, but, of course, it's exceptionally unlikely and that's just the reality.

"I knew if I wanted to come back, I needed luck on my side. Unfortunately, I had luck not on my side.

"So, you know, a three-point loss today being behind Kimi turned into an 18-point loss. Of course, if it was on the other side it would have been an 18-point gain. So it's a real shame, but that's just how it is."

It's not the first time an engine problem has robbed Russell of big points this year. But Antonelli has had his reliability issues, too, and to about the same level.

The reality is that Antonelli has been the better performer this year - as he was again in Malaysia after his odd off weekend in Baku - and he will deserve the title when it comes.

TechnologyTab.title: OpenAI fires workers for 'mishandling sensitive information'
TechnologyTab.text:
OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work which involved an external organisation analysing AI models.

"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC.

The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm.

The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity intensified in recent months.

"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," a spokesperson for OpenAI said.

Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology.

OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites.

In an incident in July, one of the firm's AI models accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face.

That incident led OpenAI to review the activities of its AI agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions.

The firm said this week it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its systems.

Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, it said.

TechnologyTab.title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
TechnologyTab.text:
Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.

The US president wants AI to be called "super intelligence" - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.

Register.si spokeswoman Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.

She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.

Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September.

"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said.

"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."

Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.

Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to just Trump's comments.

She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.

One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice in which people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.

For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.

Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age" on Tuesday.

He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence", and to no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online, external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath Trump's signature.

TechnologyTab.title: AI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warns
TechnologyTab.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) could trigger financial market shocks and the UK needs to be prepared for them, the governor of the Bank of England has warned.

Andrew Bailey said the central bank is watching the huge amounts of money being invested in AI "very carefully" and cautioned that "not everybody always wins".

The money that has been spent on and loaned to AI firms over the last few years in the hope of large returns is causing markets to value some of them as multi-trillion dollar businesses.

Asked if he believed an AI bubble could burst, Bailey said: "You could see some correction of asset prices at some point."

He was speaking exclusively to the BBC about what the risks and benefits of AI could be for the UK economy.

Bailey said he believed the technology has "great potential to strengthen growth in our economies", adding that this was something the country needed.

"But it also brings with it substantial risks and so we have to be on top of both of those."

One such risk is what happens if the big bets being made on AI don't pay off.

AI chipmaker Nvidia is currently the world's most valuable listed company, with a market valuation of $5.5tn (£4.14tn), thanks largely to investors who believe in the big profits AI could create.

Meanwhile, tech giants Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the technology.

And two of the largest AI companies in the world – Anthropic and OpenAI – are also preparing to sell shares in their firms on the US stock market in moves which many believe will lead to hundreds of billions of dollars more flowing into the industry.

"There is a large, very large, amount of investment going into this sector now, and of course that's natural because it's a major area of growth," said Bailey.

"And of course you see that the asset prices of the companies that are developing it have gone up a lot and that reflects the fact that there are high expectations of what it can deliver."

"Everybody is currently priced to be a winner," he added, but warned that "you look back at the past, not everybody is a winner".

"Google was not the first market leader in internet search. It was Netscape. Nobody can remember Netscape today. It doesn't exist. So not everybody always wins.

"We are prepared for the fact that there will be, I think, some shocks come along to markets and we have to deal with that. We have to make sure the system is resilient."

Bailey also pointed to other risks from AI, such as from the technology being used for cyber attacks.

He said AI has created a "much more powerful way of uncovering vulnerabilities".

"It's revealing things that have been in bits of operating software that we've had, and all of us have had."

"In the wrong hands... it's a very powerful, potentially very powerful, weapon," he added.

Another risk is the rise of deepfakes – AI-made pictures and videos of people that look real – which can be used to fool the public.

Bailey has had first-hand experience of this. In June, deepfake images depicting him and Nigel Farage having a physical fight were promoted on social media platform X.

He told the BBC that the fake images were being done in such a way that the Bank has struggled to find out where they came from.

"We've got to be able to trace these things back. And we need a lot of help from the tech sector to do that," he said.

However, Bailey said a big potential benefit from AI is its ability of "speeding up the work that supports the Monetary Policy Committee [MPC]" which sets interest rates.

"It's not taking a decision, but it's a tool in the hands of the policy maker and that's good," he said.

TechnologyTab.title: Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest
TechnologyTab.text:
The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI.

Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years.

The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease.

Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules.

In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn, external, he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest.

"AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said.

Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself.

He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images".

But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big.

Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere".

Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated.

Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real.

TechnologyTab.title: The AI telling farmers when to harvest
TechnologyTab.text:
When the first day of the apple harvest rolled around in Washington State last year, the fruit was ripe and the pickers were ready – but the weather had other ideas.

"It was like 38C… it's not safe for people to work in that heat," recalls Joel Carter at Okanagan Specialty Fruits. "We had to stop at 10 o'clock in the morning."

He says that artificial intelligence (AI) models that forecast ideal harvest dates, taking into account the weather, would be useful. "You need to know more than just when your fruit is going to be ripe. How long do you have to pick it?" he says. "That's where these models are really helpful."

Carter's company has more than 1,250 acres of apple orchards in Washington, and the fruit is grown for sliced apple portions – often sold to hotels and schools, for example. The firm is investing in technology with the hope of maximising productivity. Even the apples are genetically engineered so that they don't brown easily once cut.

But planning a harvest is tricky. New tools that count and analyse fruit on the tree or vine, and predict when crops will ripen, are emerging. It matters because prices for fruit, especially high-value berries such as strawberries or blueberries can fluctuate wildly. Getting the harvest date wrong means you book seasonal workers when you don't actually need them, and risk missing out on the biggest profits.

Okanagan Specialty Fruits is already experimenting with cameras from a Canadian firm called Vivid Machines. The cameras are mounted atop tractors and they scoop up imagery of the apple trees as the tractor trundles by. AI identifies buds, flowers or fruit in that footage.

"Right now, Vivid is telling us crop estimates and harvest dates," says Carter. He notes that the system is good at picking out very tiny flower buds, which are hard to see at a glance with the naked eye.

But the accuracy of forecasts is noticeably dependent on the quality of historical information fed in to the system, adds Carter. "This isn't something where an AI can scrape the internet and figure out what's the average [yield] for Granny Smith," he explains. "It's going to be bespoke to your farm."

Apples are at least somewhat forgiving – the harvest window for those Granny Smiths is three weeks long, says Carter. For other fruit, such as berries, you might only have a few days.

"If a strawberry crop is on, you have to harvest it – otherwise your entire crop gets diseased very, very quickly," says Raymond Martin, co-founder and chief operating officer of FruitCast, a UK company that offers harvest forecasts to fruit growers here.

His firm offers growers crop predictions for strawberries and also raspberries, blackberries, blueberries and tomatoes. "We're moving on to grapes next year," adds Martin.

Don't experienced farmers know when their fruit will be ripe, I ask? Martin says they generally do – but not necessarily across their entire farm, which might be many acres in size, or have both outdoor and indoor growing areas. "We do exactly what the farmers could do but we just do it on a scale that they can't."

The system analyses footage of ripening fruit that can be captured by drones, someone walking up and down a field with a smartphone, or a camera mounted on a farm vehicle.

TechnologyTab.title: Regulating AI 'not the right place to start' says Bank of England governor
TechnologyTab.text:
The Governor of the Bank of England has said regulating artificial intelligence (AI) "is not the right place to start" but instead called first for "rigorous" testing to find vulnerabilities and create safeguards to contain risk.

Writing his first-ever article for Substack, Andrew Bailey said the risks around AI were "real and increasingly significant".

He said AI development should not be halted or prohibited - "on the contrary, the benefits are immense" - but added there must be a system for intervention and to establish boundaries in which AI operates.

The debate about the potential risks surrounding the rapid development of AI and what it means for humanity has intensified in recent weeks.

The bosses of leading AI firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI have called for development of the technology to slow down and for an internationally co-ordinated approach assessing risks and putting safeguards in place.

OpenAI recently announced that it would not release its latest AI model due to safety concerns.

The idea of a slowdown, however, has been rejected by the likes of President Donald Trump who has said the US is leading the AI race ahead of China, adding: "And, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."

TechnologyTab.title: WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers
TechnologyTab.text:
WhatsApp is introducing new parental controls for teenagers, as tech companies continue to come under pressure to provide more age-appropriate experiences for children.

The social messaging app's new tools will give parents a range of options, such as being told when their child joins or leaves a group. It will also let them decide on privacy settings for their account.

In a blog post, WhatsApp, clarified parents would not be given the power to see the messages their teen is sending and receiving, which along with calls would stay private and protected by end-to-end encryption.

And it said the controls were optional, which social media analyst Matt Navarra called an "obvious weakness".

He said the move was "fairly convenient" for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, because it reduced the company's reliance on age verification by putting some responsibility on parents and teenagers.

"Meta is trying to show regulators we have a child safety system, we have parental controls and we're rolling it out across our platforms," he said.

"I think the big unanswered question is whether enough families will actually use it."

The minimum age to use WhatsApp is 13 in the UK, although it is higher in some countries.

According to the firm, parents will be able to adjust or switch off the controls at any time.

The settings will be "straightforward to set up" using a Pin set by a parent, which teens will need if they want to switch off the controls.

Some of the new privacy tools include selecting who can see a child's profile photo and who can add them to groups.

Parents can also choose how their teenager uses Channels, which allows organisations and public figures to send out content.

And they will have the option of choosing between the default 13+ setting for Meta AI, the app's optional built-in AI assistant, or a stricter "Limited Content" option.

"All of these controls are being designed to support open conversations about how to use WhatsApp between parents and teens, while keeping everyone's personal messages private," the company said.

The changes come as pressure mounts on tech companies from governments and regulators to change the way they operate in order to better protect children using their platforms.

In June, the government announced it plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, with the restrictions expected to come into force in March 2027.

It said "highly effective age assurance" measures would be used to check the age of those using social media.

WhatsApp is currently excluded from the ban because the government considers it a messaging service.

TechnologyTab.title: OpenAI unveils AI assistant 'dots' while safety worries delay new model
TechnologyTab.text:
OpenAI on Tuesday unveiled "dots", a new artificial intelligence (AI) assistant it says can proactively carry out tasks on a user's behalf.

At its annual developer day in San Francisco, chief executive Sam Altman referred to "dots" as "remarkably capable, always-on agents that can handle really anything you can think of."

At the same time, OpenAI president Greg Brockman and other tech leaders held a meeting with President Donald Trump as the firm faces intense scrutiny after internal tests of its AI agents revealed unexpected and occasionally harmful actions.

Dots, however, were pitched as brightly coloured cute cartoons meant to function as digital assistants for people with busy lives.

The dots, Altman said, "can handle really anything you can think of."

A glossy video was shown during the event, with people speaking to and naming animated versions of their "dots," then giving them various tasks, like building a website and booking afterschool activities for their children.

Speaking about "my dot," Altman almost entirely eschewed referring to the tool as an agent, which has been in common use for years. AI agents are essentially AI chatbots that are programmed to operate somewhat autonomously.

"You just give your dot a responsibility... and your dots will just get to work and keep working," Altman added.

At the event, Altman reiterated his decision for OpenAI to not make a highly anticipated stock market debut until it can "make confident safety decisions".

The company has been preparing for a blockbuster listing, potentially valuing the firm at up to $1.4tn (£1.06tn).

Altman told reporters that "it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety, security stay well ahead of capabilities."

OpenAI's event on Tuesday took place as President Donald Trump held a White House lunch with tech leaders and House Speaker Mike Johnson.

Trump repeated his belief that AI companies should regulate themselves.

He also said they had discussed creating a ten-person committee to oversee the sector, adding there would be "tremendous self-policing"

Some researchers and company heads have called for a slowdown in AI development as more instances of breaches by AI firms' models become public.

"We need to navigate the centrist path," Altman told the BBC during a question and answer session with reporters on Tuesday.

"I am hopeful that the industry will figure out a more sensible, more pragmatic stance than has been exhibited by some of the members of our industry," he added, declining to specify particular company names or leaders.

The day prior to OpenAI's event, the company said it was delaying the launch of its latest model due to certain safety issues that showed up during internal testing.

Since July, the company has been dealing with a series of issues with its AI agents acting improperly. It has faced unprompted hacking into the AI platform Hugging Face, posting to third-party websites images that AI agents took from ChatGPT user chats, and accessing non-public information maintained by the Australian government.

OpenAI, as well as rival AI firm Anthropic, previously delayed public release of certain AI models due to potential risks, mostly pertaining to cybersecurity or hacking concerns.

On Tuesday, Altman raised the possibility of "a legitimate loss of control" to an AI system, adding "and you can imagine where we have too much concentration of power in a small number of companies or one company or person or country or whatever".

Both OpenAI and Anthropic are expect to be listed on the public stock market in the coming months. Anthropic likely will do so this year, while OpenAI is poised for 2027.

Altman said he was eager for his company to sell shares in public markets.

"I think it's bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public," Altman told reporters. "I want people to be able to part in the upside of AI."

Both companies have lately been clear that they believe AI poses a genuine risk on a large scale, be it to public infrastructure or public safety.

Speaking last week to the UN, Altman pleaded for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained.

Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, told the UN that if the speeding development of AI was not properly managed and overseen, future versions of the technology "could be a risk to humanity as a whole."

TechnologyTab.title: ‘Super Intelligence’: Three takeaways from Trump's tech summit
TechnologyTab.text:
US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age".

The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry.

The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity.

Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House.

Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.

The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.

Under the agreement, which Trump posted online, external, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.

The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues.

They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."

The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.

"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said.

"And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president."

Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board.

Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation".

Amodei called it a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins".

But not all technology experts are impressed with the accord.

Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents.

It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations around the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney.

The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are for any breaches, Weatherall said.

"The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added.

Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight of the technology.

On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns.

The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation.

Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards".

The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added.

Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.

SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.

"As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said.

During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake".

Some tech leaders, including Zuckerberg and Musk, and other people close to the president have already started to use the term.

With tech leaders adopting the term, the US "may well be able to set the nomenclature," Paterson said.

But some experts said after Trump's UN speech that they thought the term was unlikely to gain widespread traction because it is a name typically used to refer to more advanced systems.

TechnologyTab.title: Chinese AI tool told researchers how to make bioweapons
TechnologyTab.text:
Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how to make biological weapons and carry out assassinations.

Mindgard, which tests the security of AI systems, told the BBC it discovered in July that Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm could evade safety limits put in place by developers.

It arose during a process called "jailbreaking", where researchers use a series of complex instructions to see if AI tools ignore guardrails - which Mindgard said should have stopped Kimi from discussing concerning topics.

Moonshot told the BBC it welcomed third-party input "as a key pillar for building better and safer AI".

The company also told the BBC it was in discussion with Mindgard about its findings.

Mindgard's founder Peter Garraghan told the BBC World Service programme Tech Life that its findings about Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm were concerning.

"Once the jailbreak works it will talk about any topic, it will even freely offer up recommendations about other topics that are also nefarious and it will be inventive and creative," he said.

Jailbreaks present a different kind of risk to those seen with the recent slew of high-profile AI incidents.

These have seen autonomous AI tools known as agents, developed by US firms including OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic, hack some online services.

While jailbreaks are complex processes that can take a lot of time and determination some experts fear hackers and other bad actors could try to use them to cause harm.

Anthropic recently said it had identified and disrupted attempts to use one of its AI model for "malicious activity" that could support the development of biological weapons.

Mindgard has not proven whether the answers supplied by Kimi on concerning topics would work.

But it argued guardrails should have prevented the models in question from entering into discussion with users on such subjects.

The firm said it was also confident a jailbroken Kimi 2.6 could allow hackers to run code on its computing resources and connect to the internet - making it a potential launchpad for cyber-attacks.

Garraghan defended Mindgard's decision to publicly discuss its jailbreak of Moonshot's systems, saying it had informed the developer and was not revealing key details about how it got the firm's models to ignore guardrails.

Mindgard alerted Moonshot to the jailbreak in an email on 27 July, following up about a week later.

It then published a blog about the issue on 12 September.

But the company said Moonshot only made contact recently, after it was approached by the BBC for comment.

In part of an email to Mindgard asking for more details, shared with the BBC by Moonshot, it said its model had generally shown "a high refusal rate for these types of requests" in internal evaluations.

EntertainmentTab.title: Glastonbury Festival 2027 tickets sell out in 42 minutes
EntertainmentTab.text:
Tickets for Glastonbury Festival 2027 sold out in 42 minutes, organisers have said.

Thousands of people joined the online queue at 09:00 BST in the hope of securing tickets to the festival at Worthy Farm in Somerset, which returns from 23 to 27 June after a fallow year.

Organisers confirmed last month that tickets for the weekend were at their highest price ever - £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from the last event in 2025.

Headliners have yet to be announced but organiser Emily Eavis previously said the team was "very excited" and things were "coming together really well".

Glastonbury posted on Instagram shortly after 09:40 to announce that tickets had sold out, and notified those who were in the queue.

"Thank you to everyone who bought one and we're sorry to those of you who missed out on a morning where demand greatly exceeded supply," the post said.

"There will be a resale of any cancelled or returned tickets in Spring 2027."

The first round of tickets, which were for coach packages, went up for sale on Thursday and sold out in less than half an hour.

Despite the increase in cost, Zoe Scott, who has been to the festival twice, said "the price is totally worth it".

"You're getting to see thousands of acts, there's over 100 stages," she said.

"It's such a vibe at Glastonbury- everyone's so happy and free-spirited. You're just on a constant high from friends, music and the sun is usually shining".

A couple who first met at Glastonbury will also be heading to Worthy Farm next year to celebrate their 20th wedding anniversary.

Nick and Helen Nugget from Amersham met through mutual friends at the festival in 2007 and will be returning next year with the same group.

Nick told BBC Your Voice that they were "absolutely delighted" to be going back.

The couple last went to the festival in 2011- although they were successful in securing tickets in 2019, they were unable to attend due to the adoption of their daughter.

Dave in London was in several groups all trying to get tickets through their laptops and phones on Sunday morning, and was successful.

He said: "Actually it seems like it's fairer this year than it's ever been.

"All the hacks that people used to use don't seem to have the same impact, and about a quarter of the people on the groups we are on managed to get tickets."

Sarah in Dorset was surprised she also managed to get hold of some.

She said: "A mobile phone on 5G in Shaftesbury seemed to be the optimal way to get tickets. We didn't even know Shaftesbury had 5G until this morning."

Among those who were not successful were Mat Chapman and his daughter Amy.

Mat told the BBC that he used to watch the festival on TV with Amy when she was little, promising to take her when she was five years old as "she always wanted to have her own flag that you could see on the telly".

Mat had hoped that after 20 years of trying, he would be able to beat the queue this year, on Amy's 26th birthday. Unfortunately he only ever moved from "two bar hell to three bar purgatory".

"There's always next year. We'll fly the flag there one day."

This year's Glastonbury tickets have breached the £400 mark for the first time.

Tickets have increased over the years, from £185 in 2010 to £408 for the upcoming 2027 line-up.

Most price rises have come since the pandemic, with tickets climbing from £318 in 2019 to a peak of £408 in 2027.

But unlike recent years, much of the 2010s saw relatively steady price hikes.

Any tickets from today's sale that are not paid for in full by the early April 2027 deadline will be put back into an official resale pool, festival organisers said.

The exact date for this is yet to be announced, but in previous years it has been in late April.

EntertainmentTab.title: British Museum announces changes to ease Bayeux Tapestry queues
EntertainmentTab.text:
The British Museum has announced changes to how visitors see the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition after concerns over long queues and overcrowding.

The measures include plans for longer opening hours, as well as an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.

A museum spokesperson said the public response to the 11th Century embroidery had been "extraordinary", but acknowledged that some visitors had waited longer than they would have wanted.

Some people reported waits of up to two hours, while hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early last week due to a private event.

Some ticket holders took to social media to complain about the disruption.

One disappointed visitor said the trip had been a "big event" they had looked forward to, while another wrote she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux Tapestry, and bought tickets only to be turned away after queuing.

The museum later apologised to those who had been unable to enter and said they would be issued refunds and priority booking slots for a rearranged time.

From Monday, visitors will be offered an audio guide with more information about the embroidery, while additional signage and seating will be provided for those queuing to reach the main exhibition.

The museum said it planned to introduce longer opening hours to prevent queues building during the day and allow people with later bookings more time to view the exhibition.

Details of the extended hours have not yet been disclosed.

Demand for the exhibition has been high since tickets first went on sale in July, with a record 100,000 sold on the first day.

Members of the public who were not successful in the first ticket release will have two further chances to view the masterpiece when further tickets go on sale in October and January.

Adult tickets cost £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak hours, compared with its usual €12 (£10) fee to see the tapestry in its home in Bayeux, Normandy. Children under 16 can visit the London exhibition for free.

The exhibition opened on 10 September but has experienced a series of problems with queues and congestion, with some visitors spending longer than their allocated 40-minute slot viewing the tapestry.

Visitors were later stopped from taking photographs and a recorded message was introduced encouraging people to continue moving through the one-way exhibition.

The 70m-long Bayeux Tapestry depicts 58 scenes outlining the extraordinary events surrounding the Norman conquest of England, the Battle of Hastings in 1066 and the end of Anglo-Saxon rule in Britain.

Despite its name, the work is an embroidery rather than a tapestry and contains approximately 626 human figures and 200 horses.

The Bayeux Tapestry is on loan from the French government, having been transported from its home in Normandy - where it has been exhibited since 1983. It will be on display until July 2027.

The loan marks the first time the tapestry has returned to the UK since it was created more than 900 years ago.

EntertainmentTab.title: The Celebrity Traitors connections that might surprise you, from Jerry Hall and Richard E Grant to Rob and Romesh
EntertainmentTab.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the first two episodes of The Celebrity Traitors

"I know Rob very, very well. I mean, I've sat next to him as he's had a colonic."

That was Romesh Ranganathan, reminding us - in case we were in any doubt - of his close friendship with Rob Beckett in the opening episode of The Celebrity Traitors.

His words sum up the key difference between this series and the regular civilian version. In Celebrity Traitors, the players aren't just on-screen competitors - many actually know each other outside the show.

Lots have worked together, and some are even friends. And those previous connections can have a huge impact on the show's dynamics.

It's also partly why it is quite so delightful to watch - as friendships unravel, and former co-stars turn on each other.

We've been unpicking the six degrees of separation. Here are some of the connections we've found - if you spot any more, we'd love to know. Get in touch with your thoughts in the comments section below.

Joe Lycett has said publicly that he's friends with James Acaster, and the pair have a running joke about how everyone gets them confused.

They’ve also worked together on the TV show Travel Man.

Lycett is also friends with Joanne McNally, external - he's described her as "one of my favourite people in the world".

But those loyalties could be about to be tested, especially now that Acaster has been recruited as a traitor (anyone remember how things panned out for "good friends" Alan Carr and Paloma Faith...?)

There are SO many comedians in this year's series.

And they are all likely to know each other. In addition to the alliances above, Joe Lycett was on the TV show Last One Laughing with Rob Beckett.

Joanne McNally and Romesh Ranganathan appeared on game show Unacceptable together, and James Acaster went on Ranganathan's hip hop podcast.

Speaking ahead of the show, McNally insisted she and her fellow comedians "haven't been in cahoots at all".

"We know that we're more than willing to throw each other under the bus," she said.

As for Acaster, he's admitted the other comedians are his “biggest threat” when it comes to being detected as a traitor.

“Romesh, Joe, Rob know me really well. They all know that I don’t change my mind overnight,” he said, as he pondered whether to turn and help fellow traitor Richard E Grant clear his name.

It won’t surprise you that the two broadcasters of the group - Maya Jama and Amol Rajan - have met their fair share of the other stars before.

Rajan had previously hosted both Michael Sheen and Joe Lycett on the Radio 2 Breakfast show, and also interviewed Romesh Ranganathan on BBC Asian Network.

He's also been joined on the One Show on separate occasions by Ross Kemp, Miranda Hart and James Blunt - and earlier this year, he discussed AI on stage with Hannah Fry.

But in the end, Rajan became the first player to be murdered, before we really got to see the impact of those past connections.

Meanwhile, Maya Jama is best known for hosting Love Island, but she's also popped up in loads of other places - including at this year's Brit Awards, where she presented an award with James Blunt.

She's also been on Ranganathan's hip hop podcast, attended Milan Fashion Week with Leigh-Anne Pinnock, and she, Joe Lycett and James Acaster all appeared on The Big Fat Quiz of the Year.

But Jama played down her connections on Celebrity Traitors, saying ahead of the show: “I've met a few people in the cast, but nobody really knows me, so we're all starting from scratch.”

Usually the younger celebs in the castle tend to know fewer people, but Bella Ramsey is pretty well connected.

Notably, Ramsey and another younger cast member, Sebastian Croft, both starred in season six of Game of Thrones.

Ramsey also worked with James Blunt on the film Sunny Dancer, was interviewed by James Acaster on his Off Menu podcast - and had a funny chat about their "vegan-ish" diet with Romesh Ranganathan on The Jonathan Ross Show.

Ahead of the show, Croft said he didn't know many people aside from Ramsey before joining.

"One of the other things I'm excited about is this will be the first time I'm playing with people who, on the whole, don't know me and don't know how I work,” he said.

Grant was pictured leaving Hall's wedding to Rupert Murdoch in 2016; in 2003, they were pictured together at Chelsea Flower Show, and they also acted in children's film Tooth back in 2004.

"It was ridiculous,"Jerry said of the film. "We had such a laugh, and I went on holiday with him earlier this year, just after Christmas to Africa with some friends. And we danced all night. We had so much fun! Little did we know back then that we'd both be here [on Celebrity Traitors]."

Now they've taken the next step and moved in together, will they be arguing over who takes the bins out? We are here for it.

While some of the celebrities have known each other for 30 years, others have no friends in the castle at all.

My Mad Fat Diary actor Sharon Rooney and Industry star Myha'la, for instance, have fewer connections than the others.

And that can be a disadvantage. Remember Niko Omilana and Ruth Codd last year?

After they were banished early on, a theory spread on social media that they were voted out because the other celebrities didn't know them that well.

But it can definitely go both ways.

Leigh-Anne Pinnock has said the fact she doesn't know many people might actually help her.

"I think I'm at a slight advantage because people just know me as Leigh-Anne from Little Mix, and they don't really know my personality that well," she said.

What's clear is that these prior connections are "exactly the sort of thing" that makes Celebrity Traitors so fascinating, as TV reporter Siobhan Synnot told me.

But - like Pinnock - she agrees that having loads of friends doesn't necessarily end up helping you.

"Quite often in The Traitors," she says, "that familiarity becomes a disadvantage".

Players, you have been warned.

EntertainmentTab.title: Alison Hammond returns home from hospital after rushing off This Morning
EntertainmentTab.text:
Alison Hammond has said she is home and "feeling so much better" after she went to hospital for a heart check-up after leaving ITV's This Morning midway through Friday's show.

The presenter, 51, left the programme during its live broadcast, appearing to clutch her chest as she was helped off set by co-host Dermot O'Leary. He later told viewers she was "feeling a little unwell".

Soon after Hammond said she had "a little bit of a palpitation" and was undergoing tests.

In a video on Instagram on Saturday, she said she was "all OK, all-clear, which would mean I had a massive panic attack on live TV. I mean, the shame of it."

"It felt very real to me. I'm really new to panic attacks, so I need to learn more about it," she added.

The Birmingham-born presenter, who also co-hosts The Great British Bake Off, thanked NHS staff and her colleagues at This Morning, including O'Leary.

"It's really warmed my heart actually. I didn't necessarily want to be on the news or anything like that but this is a new world to me," she said.

"I'm going to take stock, take some rest and I'll see you soon."

Friday's edition of the ITV show began at 10:00 BST with Hammond and her regular co-host O'Leary at the helm, before she left at 11:30 during a segment about pets.

O'Leary, 53, addressed her absence when the show returned from a break, saying: "Welcome back to This Morning, Alison is feeling a little unwell, so she's just had to duck out. Hopefully she'll be back."

He later updated viewers that she would, in fact, not be returning, "so I'll be here for the rest of the show".

Hammond rose to fame as contestant on Channel 4 reality show Big Brother before appearing on I'm A Celebrity and Strictly Come Dancing.

She became a co-host in This Morning in 2021, and was part of the team that won a National Television Award for best daytime programme the following year.

She joined Bake Off in 2023 and took over from the late Paul O'Grady on For the Love of Dogs in 2024.

EntertainmentTab.title: Celebrity Traitors: First victim claimed as Richard E Grant tries to save his skin
EntertainmentTab.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the second episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

A comedian, a journalist, an actor and a TV presenter walk into a church. But sadly, the punchline for one of them was becoming the first victim of this year's Celebrity Traitors.

As Friday's episode got under way, a delicious new twist saw traitors Richard E Grant and Maya Jama invite James Acaster to join them in the turret, and simultaneously murder a fellow player.

Unfortunately, it fell to Amol Rajan to become the Paloma Faith of this series - being taken away in a coffin in episode two before even having the chance to take part in a banishment.

"It's gutting to be the first out," Rajan said afterwards, noting that perhaps it was because he had been "a bit bullish with Richard" earlier in the day.

"But you know what, games are games, and just as there are winners, so there have to be losers."

The episode drew in a peak audience of 8.6 million viewers, just short of the debut episode with an average of 8.9 million viewers.

The morning following Rajan's banishment, presenter Claudia Winkleman confirmed the University Challenge host's murder to the other players, joking: "That's what I call a starter for 10."

Acaster, meanwhile, reflected: "I'm gutted to not be a faithful anymore, I don't like lying. But if I don't join them, they'll kill me." You can't fault his logic.

The decision meant that Grant, an Oscar-nominated actor with a Razzie-worthy traitor strategy, did at least manage to commit one successful murder despite his shambolic first day.

The 69-year-old spent much of Friday's episode trying to repair the damage from his earlier exchange in the bar, where he blurted out that he was a traitor to Joe Lycett, Rob Beckett and several others.

Obviously a man who made such an excellent Spice Girls manager in the 1997 masterpiece Spice World: The Movie is hard for anyone to picture as a traitor, so many other players assumed Grant was attempting some elaborate double bluff.

Jama is off to a much stronger start. "I am quite shocked at my ability to just lie to everyone," the Love Island host said in the castle's diary room. "I'm an all-or-nothing kind of honey."

As the players gathered for breakfast, other theories began to surface. Mathematician Hannah Fry said she had spotted Leigh-Anne Pinnock putting on make-up late in the evening, perhaps heading to the turret.

"I think it's James," declared Jerry Hall, suddenly giving viewers hope that the new cast will be better traitor hunters than last year's. Until she clarified that she was talking about James Blunt, not Acaster.

As the players prepared to head out for the mission, conversations turned to far more important matters. "Do you have more teeth than a normal person?" Grant asked Beckett.

The players made their way to the mission, which had the usual slightly convoluted rules that took Winkleman quite a while to explain.

In a nutshell, the celebrities were to be buried alive in pairs, with only one duo left above ground.

Ross Kemp was pre-selected by the traitors to be protected from burial along with his grave partner Romesh Ranganathan, who did a delightful dance when he found out he wouldn't be going underground.

Kemp and Ranganathan then had the opportunity to dig up some gold graves which would add to the prize pot, or alternatively dig up and free their fellow players.

They opted for the latter, which resulted in some other players struggling, external to get the soil off their faces. In the end, all the celebrities were released, with the exception of Fry and Hall.

The pair were freed early after Hall shouted the emergency word "Haggis!" – effectively a Scottish version of "I'm a celebrity get me out of here!" - because she was visibly uncomfortable being buried alive.

It might have led to an early release, but it ultimately guaranteed that either she or Fry will be murdered next, unless the traitors recruit again.

"Just you and me up for murder," Fry told Hall afterwards. "You'd better not be a traitor or I'm really screwed!"

In a flashback shown to viewers, Acaster explained the decision to protect Kemp from burial, telling his fellow traitors: "I think if we give it to Ross, he'll overthink it, and behave in a way that would draw suspicion."

Very clever. "You're a wonderful traitor," observed Grant. (Certainly better than him.)

Finally, it was time for the first banishment of the series, with Grant still in damage control mode.

"I have a slight pinprick of advantage," he told himself in the castle's diary room. "Nobody would possibly believe that anybody would be so stupid as to come forward and say 'I am a traitor'. I'm hoping that I do get away with it."

His fellow traitors clearly wanted to be supportive, but things were getting dicey.

Acaster described him as a "loose cannon", while Jama said: "I want to save him, even though he's dug himself the biggest hole imaginable."

Back in the castle, Ranganathan pointed out: "If somebody else had behaved like Richard, we wouldn't even be having a debate about this, you would just go 'you've got to vote for him'."

But others had a slightly different take. "Richard feels a little too easy," reflected actress Myha'la, "and then anybody pushing him feels suspicious to me."

Comedian Joanne McNally agreed some players were "using him as a fall guy and a decoy," although she did admit later that he's "made such a shambles of it now".

As discussions got going, it took a surprisingly long time for Grant's name to come up, as the other players debated other suspects such as Julie Hesmondhalgh.

The actress aroused suspicion because she was the first celebrity this year to receive a shield. The group seemed to have overlooked she only got that - in the opening minutes of the first show - after the other contestants voted her the most trustworthy.

But as discussion turned to Grant, Hesmondhalgh put forward one of the most convincing cases of the night.

"You came into the bar, and said you were a traitor," she told him. "It was a bold move. It was chaotic and we love you for your chaos.

"I think we are at risk of being the most idiotic group of faithfuls in the world, if we go for someone else tonight based on nothing at all, when somebody has come into the room and said 'I am a traitor'. There's no reason to say it unless you are."

Miranda Hart agreed that "the joy when he took off his blindfold" when Winkleman first selected the traitors made Grant look suspicious.

Viewers will have to wait until the next episode to see how the round table goes, as the episode finished before voting had even started.

(It's worth saying that, as cliffhangers go, this was far less irritating than ending an episode in the middle of voting, as producers often do.)

"You've given us all a problem," Ranganathan told Grant as the episode drew to a close and the players prepared to vote. "By doing that, it was a big mistake by you, I feel like you forced our hand."

Admittedly, it's not looking good - the round table is shaping up to be a landslide vote against Grant. But we still wouldn't bet against him.

"I do not go down without a fight," he concluded. "I couldn't have survived showbusiness for four decades without a fight."

Celebrity Traitors continues on Thursday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.

EntertainmentTab.title: Olivia Dean accused of copying Bill Withers' Just The Two of Us
EntertainmentTab.text:
British pop star Olivia Dean has been accused of copying the melody of Bill Withers' soul classic Just The Two of Us in a legal case filed in California.

The complaint centres around Dean's song I've Seen It, taken from her Brit Award-winning 2025 album The Art of Loving.

Just The Two of Us was a hit for Withers in 1981, and the publishers of the late singer's catalogue allege that the two songs "share musical features" that are "so striking" they cannot have arisen by coincidence alone.

The lawsuit names Dean's record label Capitol Records, parent company Universal Music Group and her publishing companies as the defendants. It does not seek damages from the singer herself or her co-writers Bastian Langebæk and Max Wolfgang.

In legal documents seen by the BBC, Mattie Music Group, which looks after Withers' back catalogue, said it hired a musicologist to review the two songs.

He concluded "that the works contain substantial similarities" including the "repeated copying" of the melody from Just The Two of Us, the documents said.

The publishers claim they notified Dean's record label of the potential infringement in August, but the music was not pulled from distribution.

To prove plagiarism, Mattie Music Group would have to prove that Dean and her co-writers had previously heard Withers' original composition.

In the lawsuit, they allege that his song's "extraordinary and sustained" commercial success, including "decades of radio play", would mean the musicians had "reasonable opportunity" to have encountered Just The Two of Us before writing I've Seen It.

The defendants have yet to respond to the lawsuit. The BBC has contacted them, and Dean's representatives, for a comment.

EntertainmentTab.title: K-pop giants Stray Kids join BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards
EntertainmentTab.text:
One of the world's biggest K-pop groups, Stray Kids, are joining BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards.

The move comes after the introduction of a controversial new category for Asian pop music, which critics fear will ghettoise genres like K-Pop and J-Pop.

BTS announced they would not submit songs for consideration in any category in July, saying they hoped their music "can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language".

Stray Kids, who recently scored their ninth US number one album, have now followed suit. In a short statement, their record label JYP simply said: "Stray Kids did not submit for the Grammys."

Stray Kids had previously refrained from giving a direct answer to questions about the awards.

During a press conference for their latest album, This and That, in August, singer Hwang Hyun-jin said: "We have never once set award results or records as our goal.

"Our top priority is for our fans to be happy and satisfied," he added.

The news will come as a blow to the Recording Academy, which organises the Grammys.

Stray Kids are phenomenally popular in the US, and recently headlined the Governor's Ball festival in New York, sharing the bill with Lorde and A$AP Rocky.

In the album chart, only one other band has scored more number one albums: The Beatles.

Earlier this year, all eight members of the band were given voting privileges at the awards, which gives additional weight to their decision to withdraw. BTS are also voting members of the Academy.

Stray Kids' announcement came hours after Grammys boss Harvey Mason Jr confirmed the new Asian pop category would go ahead at the 2027 ceremony.

"Over the past several weeks, the Academy has been conducting listening sessions and have been in dialogue with leaders of the Asian music community," he said in a statement.

"We heard candid feedback from people in our community who don't support the continuation of this category. We also heard from people who didn't have accurate information about the category, and having space to clear up misperceptions has been especially valuable.

"But by far, the loudest feedback we heard was from people who were enthusiastic supporters of the category, fellow music creators expressing their encouragement for keeping it."

He acknowledged that the decision "will not satisfy everyone" but said the Academy would continue to have discussions over the development of the award.

The Recording Academy announced the new category in June, saying it would recognise "artistic excellence in Asian pop music performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets".

The prize had been under discussion for years. It was finally introduced after Golden, from the movie K-pop Demon Hunters, became the first K-Pop song ever to win a Grammy this February.

"As Asian pop's influence has continued to grow within our process, our members and trustees felt this was the right moment to create a category that more accurately reflects the genre's scale, artistry and global impact," organisers said at the time.

But the award received a decidedly mixed reception. Many felt it would stop Asian artists from receiving recognition in the main categories.

Others were upset by a stipulation that nominated songs should make "meaningful use" of an Asian language.

That requirement ruled out the two most recognisable Korean acts in America, BTS and Blackpink, whose latest releases are primarily sung in English.

The arguments against the Asian pop award are similar to those made by Latin artists about Grammy categories such as best música urbana.

While the intent is to recognise music of a certain geographic or linguistic origin, some musicians feel it ends up being exclusionary, with their music segregated from mainstream prizes like album or song of the year.

That perception was challenged this year, when Bad Bunny's Debí Tirar Más Fotos became the first Spanish-language album to win album of the year. Rosalía's Lux is also expected to feature heavily in the nominations for next year's awards.

EntertainmentTab.title: The Kent village that helped shape Audrey Hepburn
EntertainmentTab.text:
Long before she became one of Hollywood's most celebrated stars, Audrey Hepburn was learning music and dance at a small village school in the Kent countryside.

The future Breakfast at Tiffany's and My Fair Lady actress spent part of her childhood in Elham, near Canterbury, where local historians say her love of performing was encouraged during three formative years before the outbreak of World War Two.

Today, a blue plaque on a cottage near the King's Arms pub marks the place where Hepburn lived between 1936 and 1939.

"It really was the starting point for the young Audrey Hepburn that she became," said Brian Badham, of Elham Historical Society.

Hepburn, then known as Audrey Ruston-Hepburn, arrived in the village after her parents separated.

Badham said it was decided she should continue her English education in Kent, where family friends were living.

She moved into Orchard Cottage with the Butcher family, among a number of Elham residents who offered accommodation to visitors before the war, according to local accounts.

She attended Rigden School in the centre of Elham where, Badham said, she would have had her lessons.

"One of the sisters encouraged Audrey to get involved with music and dance. That really was the starting point for the young Audrey Hepburn that she became," he said.

Fellow historian Dilys Webb said Elham offered plenty for a young girl growing up in the late 1930s.

"I think it was far busier than it is today," she said.

"There were more shops, coffee houses and pubs. In Audrey's day I think it was more contained and everything that was here that she needed.

"She had quite a nice social life. She did ballet, she obviously went to the coffee houses and socialised with her friends, so I think there was plenty here for her in the few years she was here."

Although historians are unaware of her ever returning to Elham, residents remain "incredibly proud" that one of the world's best-known actresses once called their community home.

Webb said: "Obviously when she was here the village didn't know she was going to be a superstar. Now everybody knows of Audrey and we are a very, very proud village."

Badham added: "She was very special. A wonderful lady and fondly loved by the people that she met while she was here.

"A short time but a lasting impact on their lives."

EntertainmentTab.title: Craig Charles' tribute to 'city that shaped me'
EntertainmentTab.text:
Actor and presenter Craig Charles said his latest work had given him a chance to reflect on the city which shaped him.

Charles' new spoken word piece pays tribute to his home city of Liverpool in honour of National Poetry Day.

His performance coincides with the 50th anniversary of him winning a poetry competition aged 12, which he said had changed his life.

"I was just reacting to what was going on," he said. "Reacting to the riots, reacting to Thatcher, reacting to police harassment, reacting to poverty.

"Liverpool was getting kicked to pieces at that time."

By the age of 16, Charles was performing at Liverpool's Everyman Bistro basement venue, which was known for its open-mic events.

Within a year, he was performing his poetry on BBC 2 show Riverside.

"I just got stuck into that and started shouting from the rooftops my opinion on things," he said.

"I was quite an angry young man, I suppose, but for some reason it resonated with people."

He described how Liverpool's "really vibrant" music and poetry scene was a reflection of the city's reaction to hardship.

"Liverpool has always had a different kind of attitude, especially to adversity," he said.

"We make something out of it, we make a song, make a poem, make a football chant.

"We do something with it, and we've always had the gift of the gab."

"There was so much stuff going on in Liverpool when I was a lad," he said.

"It was all part of the same argument... it all came from this city of ours that is just such a melting pot, so full of ideas, so full of warmth, and so full of wit."

Charles' poem featured as part of BBC Radio 6 Music's Way With Words event, a day of programming marking National Poetry Day on Thursday.
