articles.title: Celebrity Traitors: First victim claimed as Richard E Grant tries to save his skin
articles.text:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the second episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

A comedian, a journalist, an actor and a TV presenter walk into a church. But sadly, the punchline for one of them was becoming the first victim of this year's Celebrity Traitors.

As Friday's episode got under way, a delicious new twist saw traitors Richard E Grant and Maya Jama invite James Acaster to join them in the turret, and simultaneously murder a fellow player.

Unfortunately, it fell to Amol Rajan to become the Paloma Faith of this series - being taken away in a coffin in episode two before even having the chance to take part in a banishment.

"It's gutting to be the first out," Rajan said afterwards, noting that perhaps it was because he had been "a bit bullish with Richard" earlier in the day.

"But you know what, games are games, and just as there are winners, so there have to be losers."

The episode drew in a peak audience of 8.6 million viewers, just short of the debut episode with an average of 8.9 million viewers.

The morning following Rajan's banishment, presenter Claudia Winkleman confirmed the University Challenge host's murder to the other players, joking: "That's what I call a starter for 10."

Acaster, meanwhile, reflected: "I'm gutted to not be a faithful anymore, I don't like lying. But if I don't join them, they'll kill me." You can't fault his logic.

The decision meant that Grant, an Oscar-nominated actor with a Razzie-worthy traitor strategy, did at least manage to commit one successful murder despite his shambolic first day.

The 69-year-old spent much of Friday's episode trying to repair the damage from his earlier exchange in the bar, where he blurted out that he was a traitor to Joe Lycett, Rob Beckett and several others.

Obviously a man who made such an excellent Spice Girls manager in the 1997 masterpiece Spice World: The Movie is hard for anyone to picture as a traitor, so many other players assumed Grant was attempting some elaborate double bluff.

Jama is off to a much stronger start. "I am quite shocked at my ability to just lie to everyone," the Love Island host said in the castle's diary room. "I'm an all-or-nothing kind of honey."

As the players gathered for breakfast, other theories began to surface. Mathematician Hannah Fry said she had spotted Leigh-Anne Pinnock putting on make-up late in the evening, perhaps heading to the turret.

"I think it's James," declared Jerry Hall, suddenly giving viewers hope that the new cast will be better traitor hunters than last year's. Until she clarified that she was talking about James Blunt, not Acaster.

As the players prepared to head out for the mission, conversations turned to far more important matters. "Do you have more teeth than a normal person?" Grant asked Beckett.

The players made their way to the mission, which had the usual slightly convoluted rules that took Winkleman quite a while to explain.

In a nutshell, the celebrities were to be buried alive in pairs, with only one duo left above ground.

Ross Kemp was pre-selected by the traitors to be protected from burial along with his grave partner Romesh Ranganathan, who did a delightful dance when he found out he wouldn't be going underground.

Kemp and Ranganathan then had the opportunity to dig up some gold graves which would add to the prize pot, or alternatively dig up and free their fellow players.

They opted for the latter, which resulted in some other players struggling, external to get the soil off their faces. In the end, all the celebrities were released, with the exception of Fry and Hall.

The pair were freed early after Hall shouted the emergency word "Haggis!" – effectively a Scottish version of "I'm a celebrity get me out of here!" - because she was visibly uncomfortable being buried alive.

It might have led to an early release, but it ultimately guaranteed that either she or Fry will be murdered next, unless the traitors recruit again.

"Just you and me up for murder," Fry told Hall afterwards. "You'd better not be a traitor or I'm really screwed!"

In a flashback shown to viewers, Acaster explained the decision to protect Kemp from burial, telling his fellow traitors: "I think if we give it to Ross, he'll overthink it, and behave in a way that would draw suspicion."

Very clever. "You're a wonderful traitor," observed Grant. (Certainly better than him.)

Finally, it was time for the first banishment of the series, with Grant still in damage control mode.

"I have a slight pinprick of advantage," he told himself in the castle's diary room. "Nobody would possibly believe that anybody would be so stupid as to come forward and say 'I am a traitor'. I'm hoping that I do get away with it."

His fellow traitors clearly wanted to be supportive, but things were getting dicey.

Acaster described him as a "loose cannon", while Jama said: "I want to save him, even though he's dug himself the biggest hole imaginable."

Back in the castle, Ranganathan pointed out: "If somebody else had behaved like Richard, we wouldn't even be having a debate about this, you would just go 'you've got to vote for him'."

But others had a slightly different take. "Richard feels a little too easy," reflected actress Myha'la, "and then anybody pushing him feels suspicious to me."

Comedian Joanne McNally agreed some players were "using him as a fall guy and a decoy," although she did admit later that he's "made such a shambles of it now".

As discussions got going, it took a surprisingly long time for Grant's name to come up, as the other players debated other suspects such as Julie Hesmondhalgh.

The actress aroused suspicion because she was the first celebrity this year to receive a shield. The group seemed to have overlooked she only got that - in the opening minutes of the first show - after the other contestants voted her the most trustworthy.

But as discussion turned to Grant, Hesmondhalgh put forward one of the most convincing cases of the night.

"You came into the bar, and said you were a traitor," she told him. "It was a bold move. It was chaotic and we love you for your chaos.

"I think we are at risk of being the most idiotic group of faithfuls in the world, if we go for someone else tonight based on nothing at all, when somebody has come into the room and said 'I am a traitor'. There's no reason to say it unless you are."

Miranda Hart agreed that "the joy when he took off his blindfold" when Winkleman first selected the traitors made Grant look suspicious.

Viewers will have to wait until the next episode to see how the round table goes, as the episode finished before voting had even started.

(It's worth saying that, as cliffhangers go, this was far less irritating than ending an episode in the middle of voting, as producers often do.)

"You've given us all a problem," Ranganathan told Grant as the episode drew to a close and the players prepared to vote. "By doing that, it was a big mistake by you, I feel like you forced our hand."

Admittedly, it's not looking good - the round table is shaping up to be a landslide vote against Grant. But we still wouldn't bet against him.

"I do not go down without a fight," he concluded. "I couldn't have survived showbusiness for four decades without a fight."

Celebrity Traitors continues on Thursday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.

articles.title: Olivia Dean accused of copying Bill Withers' Just The Two of Us
articles.text:
British pop star Olivia Dean has been accused of copying the melody of Bill Withers' soul classic Just The Two of Us in a legal case filed in California.

The complaint centres around Dean's song I've Seen It, taken from her Brit Award-winning 2025 album The Art of Loving.

Just The Two of Us was a hit for Withers in 1981, and the publishers of the late singer's catalogue allege that the two songs "share musical features" that are "so striking" they cannot have arisen by coincidence alone.

The lawsuit names Dean's record label Capitol Records, parent company Universal Music Group and her publishing companies as the defendants. It does not seek damages from the singer herself or her co-writers Bastian Langebæk and Max Wolfgang.

In legal documents seen by the BBC, Mattie Music Group, which looks after Withers' back catalogue, said it hired a musicologist to review the two songs.

He concluded "that the works contain substantial similarities" including the "repeated copying" of the melody from Just The Two of Us, the documents said.

The publishers claim they notified Dean's record label of the potential infringement in August, but the music was not pulled from distribution.

To prove plagiarism, Mattie Music Group would have to prove that Dean and her co-writers had previously heard Withers' original composition.

In the lawsuit, they allege that his song's "extraordinary and sustained" commercial success, including "decades of radio play", would mean the musicians had "reasonable opportunity" to have encountered Just The Two of Us before writing I've Seen It.

The defendants have yet to respond to the lawsuit. The BBC has contacted them, and Dean's representatives, for a comment.

articles.title: K-pop giants Stray Kids join BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards
articles.text:
One of the world's biggest K-pop groups, Stray Kids, are joining BTS in boycotting the 2027 Grammy Awards.

The move comes after the introduction of a controversial new category for Asian pop music, which critics fear will ghettoise genres like K-Pop and J-Pop.

BTS announced they would not submit songs for consideration in any category in July, saying they hoped their music "can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language".

Stray Kids, who recently scored their ninth US number one album, have now followed suit. In a short statement, their record label JYP simply said: "Stray Kids did not submit for the Grammys."

Stray Kids had previously refrained from giving a direct answer to questions about the awards.

During a press conference for their latest album, This and That, in August, singer Hwang Hyun-jin said: "We have never once set award results or records as our goal.

"Our top priority is for our fans to be happy and satisfied," he added.

The news will come as a blow to the Recording Academy, which organises the Grammys.

Stray Kids are phenomenally popular in the US, and recently headlined the Governor's Ball festival in New York, sharing the bill with Lorde and A$AP Rocky.

In the album chart, only one other band has scored more number one albums: The Beatles.

Earlier this year, all eight members of the band were given voting privileges at the awards, which gives additional weight to their decision to withdraw. BTS are also voting members of the Academy.

Stray Kids' announcement came hours after Grammys boss Harvey Mason Jr confirmed the new Asian pop category would go ahead at the 2027 ceremony.

"Over the past several weeks, the Academy has been conducting listening sessions and have been in dialogue with leaders of the Asian music community," he said in a statement.

"We heard candid feedback from people in our community who don't support the continuation of this category. We also heard from people who didn't have accurate information about the category, and having space to clear up misperceptions has been especially valuable.

"But by far, the loudest feedback we heard was from people who were enthusiastic supporters of the category, fellow music creators expressing their encouragement for keeping it."

He acknowledged that the decision "will not satisfy everyone" but said the Academy would continue to have discussions over the development of the award.

The Recording Academy announced the new category in June, saying it would recognise "artistic excellence in Asian pop music performances originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets".

The prize had been under discussion for years. It was finally introduced after Golden, from the movie K-pop Demon Hunters, became the first K-Pop song ever to win a Grammy this February.

"As Asian pop's influence has continued to grow within our process, our members and trustees felt this was the right moment to create a category that more accurately reflects the genre's scale, artistry and global impact," organisers said at the time.

But the award received a decidedly mixed reception. Many felt it would stop Asian artists from receiving recognition in the main categories.

Others were upset by a stipulation that nominated songs should make "meaningful use" of an Asian language.

That requirement ruled out the two most recognisable Korean acts in America, BTS and Blackpink, whose latest releases are primarily sung in English.

The arguments against the Asian pop award are similar to those made by Latin artists about Grammy categories such as best música urbana.

While the intent is to recognise music of a certain geographic or linguistic origin, some musicians feel it ends up being exclusionary, with their music segregated from mainstream prizes like album or song of the year.

That perception was challenged this year, when Bad Bunny's Debí Tirar Más Fotos became the first Spanish-language album to win album of the year. Rosalía's Lux is also expected to feature heavily in the nominations for next year's awards.

articles.title: The Kent village that helped shape Audrey Hepburn
articles.text:
Long before she became one of Hollywood's most celebrated stars, Audrey Hepburn was learning music and dance at a small village school in the Kent countryside.

The future Breakfast at Tiffany's and My Fair Lady actress spent part of her childhood in Elham, near Canterbury, where local historians say her love of performing was encouraged during three formative years before the outbreak of World War Two.

Today, a blue plaque on a cottage near the King's Arms pub marks the place where Hepburn lived between 1936 and 1939.

"It really was the starting point for the young Audrey Hepburn that she became," said Brian Badham, of Elham Historical Society.

Hepburn, then known as Audrey Ruston-Hepburn, arrived in the village after her parents separated.

Badham said it was decided she should continue her English education in Kent, where family friends were living.

She moved into Orchard Cottage with the Butcher family, among a number of Elham residents who offered accommodation to visitors before the war, according to local accounts.

She attended Rigden School in the centre of Elham where, Badham said, she would have had her lessons.

"One of the sisters encouraged Audrey to get involved with music and dance. That really was the starting point for the young Audrey Hepburn that she became," he said.

Fellow historian Dilys Webb said Elham offered plenty for a young girl growing up in the late 1930s.

"I think it was far busier than it is today," she said.

"There were more shops, coffee houses and pubs. In Audrey's day I think it was more contained and everything that was here that she needed.

"She had quite a nice social life. She did ballet, she obviously went to the coffee houses and socialised with her friends, so I think there was plenty here for her in the few years she was here."

Although historians are unaware of her ever returning to Elham, residents remain "incredibly proud" that one of the world's best-known actresses once called their community home.

Webb said: "Obviously when she was here the village didn't know she was going to be a superstar. Now everybody knows of Audrey and we are a very, very proud village."

Badham added: "She was very special. A wonderful lady and fondly loved by the people that she met while she was here.

"A short time but a lasting impact on their lives."

articles.title: Craig Charles' tribute to 'city that shaped me'
articles.text:
Actor and presenter Craig Charles said his latest work had given him a chance to reflect on the city which shaped him.

Charles' new spoken word piece pays tribute to his home city of Liverpool in honour of National Poetry Day.

His performance coincides with the 50th anniversary of him winning a poetry competition aged 12, which he said had changed his life.

"I was just reacting to what was going on," he said. "Reacting to the riots, reacting to Thatcher, reacting to police harassment, reacting to poverty.

"Liverpool was getting kicked to pieces at that time."

By the age of 16, Charles was performing at Liverpool's Everyman Bistro basement venue, which was known for its open-mic events.

Within a year, he was performing his poetry on BBC 2 show Riverside.

"I just got stuck into that and started shouting from the rooftops my opinion on things," he said.

"I was quite an angry young man, I suppose, but for some reason it resonated with people."

He described how Liverpool's "really vibrant" music and poetry scene was a reflection of the city's reaction to hardship.

"Liverpool has always had a different kind of attitude, especially to adversity," he said.

"We make something out of it, we make a song, make a poem, make a football chant.

"We do something with it, and we've always had the gift of the gab."

"There was so much stuff going on in Liverpool when I was a lad," he said.

"It was all part of the same argument... it all came from this city of ours that is just such a melting pot, so full of ideas, so full of warmth, and so full of wit."

Charles' poem featured as part of BBC Radio 6 Music's Way With Words event, a day of programming marking National Poetry Day on Thursday.

articles.title: How photographer Tim Smith captured Bradford's daytime dance revolution
articles.text:
For decades, photographer Tim Smith's images of Bradford's British Asian "daytimers" dance scene remained largely unseen. Now, some of those shots are taking their place in a major Tate exhibition examining the creativity and rebellion that transformed 1990s Britain.

On a bright afternoon in Bradford, shoppers moved through the city centre carrying bags, going about their day.

Behind a nearby doorway, another side of Bradford was pulsing to a very different rhythm.

Tim Smith remembers stepping out of a small nightclub beneath the Alhambra theatre after spending hours photographing a "daytimers" disco.

"I walked out into this bright sunshine and there's all these people walking about with their shopping bags, completely oblivious to what was going on just the other side of this somewhat anonymous-looking doorway," he recalls.

More than three decades later, images Smith took inside that hidden world are making another unlikely journey, from Bradford's underground daytimers scene to the Tate Britain art gallery.

His photographs feature in new showcase The 90s: Art and Fashion, which opens on Thursday.

Curated by former Vogue editor-in-chief Edward Enninful, it brings together more than 100 works by nearly 70 artists, photographers and designers to examine a decade of creativity and rebellion.

For Smith, who lived in Bradford for more than 40 years, the inclusion of his photos is also recognition that some of the cultural shifts reshaping 1990s Britain were happening far beyond London.

"I'm pleased because I think there's a big shout-out for Bradford," he says.

"These culturally significant moments of that time weren't just happening in London and Manchester, like many media people like to think they were."

Smith arrived in Bradford in the mid-1980s after studying photography in Newport.

A nomadic childhood and life among migrant communities in Newport's Docklands had drawn him towards documenting lives beyond the mainstream.

Through the then-recently established Bradford Heritage Recording Unit, he began photographing the city's South Asian communities at work, at religious gatherings, at weddings and in their social lives.

"I was quite appalled at the lack of any kind of documentation of Bradford's Asian communities beyond the stuff that you'd see in the local papers," he says.

The daytimers bhangra gigs came later, after a friend told him about afternoon club events for young British Asians.

Smith's first response was simple: "What's a daytimer?"

He soon found out.

Cheap to hire while nightclubs stood empty during the day, the venues became spaces where a generation could gather and celebrate, but also shape a unique new subculture: dancing to music drawing on Punjabi and South Asian traditions but fused with contemporary British sounds.

What Smith saw was not simply young people celebrating being Asian, but proudly "being British Asian".

Among those he photographed was Rani Kaur, known as DJ Radical Sister, one of the pioneering women of the scene.

In one of Smith's best-known images, which will feature in the Tate Britain exhibition, she stands at the DJ decks, surrounded by young clubbers.

Another frame, shot from above in the darkness with flash, caught a room full of faces in a moment Smith could not inspect until the film was developed.

"Part of it's luck, but you earn your luck," he says.

"Every single face that you can see in it… just looks like he's having the best time of his life."

To Smith, the expressions seem to say: "We're here, this is us, we're having a wonderful time."

Yet he appreciates there is another side to the photographs, and to the rebellion they record.

Many of the young people attending daytimers gigs were moving between the expectations of family and community and the desires of a younger generation testing out music, fashion, friendship and independence on its own terms.

Smith understood that publishing a photograph could expose somebody who had never intended their presence at a club to become public.

"I didn't know everybody in the picture," he says. "I thought, 'I don't want to get them into trouble.'"

So, apart from images of people he knew were comfortable being identified, much of the work stayed largely out of public view.

Only decades later did those photographs acquire another life.

When some were exhibited at Bradford's National Science and Media Museum, there were, Smith recalls, "one or two grumblings".

But among those who had lived through the scene there was also a growing sense that this was their history to claim.

"Come on, it was our moment," was the response relayed back to him. "This is where who we are now began."

Time has now transformed the pictures from informal snapshots of an underground scene into historical documents.

And Smith believes the daytimers helped lay the foundations for the vibrant British Asian culture scene that followed.

He was, by his own admission, entering worlds that were not his, a young white photographer trusted with access to communities and spaces whose stories were rarely documented.

"I felt quite privileged being a photographer generally because it gives you access to worlds that aren't necessarily part of your world," he says.

"I loved being let in."

Now those darkened daytime Bradford rooms will take their place alongside other defining names and moments in cultural history inside Tate Britain, home to the biggest collection of British art in the world.

For Smith, there is real satisfaction in that journey: from an anonymous doorway in Bradford to one of the country's great national galleries.

It is also a recognition that while much of the cultural establishment looked elsewhere, Bradford was slowly writing a cultural history of its own, and continues to do so.

articles.title: London film festival celebrates British-Latino identity
articles.text:
An event billed as London's only competitive Latino film festival is now under way for the first time in the capital.

Venues including the Barbican, the ICA, Ciné Lumière and BFI Stephen Street will screen 60 films from 27 countries until Tuesday.

There will also be workshops and performances with guests including Cuban dancer Carlos Acosta, a former principal at the Royal Ballet, Argentine actor Óscar Martínez, Cuban actor Jorge Perugorría and Oscar-winning Chilean screenwriter Gonzalo Maza.

The event was founded by Cuban actress Ketty Rodriguez who, when she moved to London, was struck by the lack of Latin representation in a city famous for its multiculturalism, film and history.

She told BBC London: "Everything here is about community, is about connection, and the idea started because I couldn't find my people, I didn't know where they were, so I decided to do this festival and it's very successful, I'm very happy."

Rodriguez says it is the first competitive Latino film festival of this size in London.

"We have received hundreds of entries from all over Latin America, and can't wait to support and showcase features, documentaries, animation, and shorts from these incredible filmmakers," she said.

Cuban dancer Javier Torres, who developed the festival idea with Rodriguez, said: "This is just the start of something great. We found a gap in the market, we found a necessity of the Latino community to come together and to give voice and narrative voices to Latin American filmmakers.

"This is a platform for diplomacy, for culture, to get together and this is what we are building here."

Alongside entries from Latin America are stories made in London for Londoners.

Victor Rios, a British-Bolivian filmmaker said the event was a chance "not just to celebrate people of Latin roots but also to celebrate British-Latino identity".

He moved to the UK at 16, and has two short films in the selection.

He said: "It's very crucial for people to understand that we are not just here passing by. We are part of society, and this festival is establishing that too.

"We're very proud to be Colombians, Bolivians, Ecuadorians, Peruvians, Chileans, but we are also British.

"So we have a place, we have a say, and we want to be heard."

The festival is backed by the BFI through National Lottery funding and by the City of London Corporation.

articles.title: ‘If it’s too slick, it looks like a fashion mag’: Peter Zumthor on his £110m rammed concrete gallery
articles.text:
In the early 1960s, when Peter Zumthor was a teenage apprentice in his father’s cabinet-making workshop, he designed his first cupboard. He later recalled the satisfaction of fitting the door so perfectly that it closed “with a special sucking sound”, saying his father instilled in him “the Basel pride in the well-built object”.

Six decades on, with a fleet of globally celebrated projects to his name, the 83-year-old Swiss architect is back in Basel, beaming with the same local pride. He is gazing out at his latest well-built object, which is also his first project here: a monolithic new gallery that looks chiselled from the earth, its layers of pale crumbly concrete hammered into shape, its big oak and bronze doors – their handles wrapped with leather cord – closing with that same satisfyingly expensive Swiss swoosh.

“It was an old feeling,” Zumthor tells me, describing working in his home town to build the £110m addition to the Beyeler Foundation. “I encountered craftspeople who remembered my father, who had this special knowledge of how to make things. They weren’t surprised if something had to be custom-made.”

It was quite a change from his previous building site. Fresh from the recent opening of the tortuous, two-decade-long, $724m addition to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, Zumthor is visibly relieved to be back on home turf. “The normal American architect is used to sourcing products, not looking for somebody who can make something custom-made,” he says, with a furrowed brow. “Their buildings are an assembly of products.”

Not so in Switzerland. From the pear wood handrails to the leather benches and blown glass lamps, every piece of his new gallery has been meticulously handmade. But is the sum of these bespoke parts a worthy companion to one of the country’s – if not the world’s – most beloved art museums?

Designed by Italian architect Renzo Piano, the Beyeler Foundation was hailed as a model of elegant restraint when it opened in October 1997 – the same month as Frank Gehry’s billowing Bilbao Guggenheim – praised as a sober foil to the “iconic” tendencies of the time. Sited in Riehen, just outside Basel, in the grounds of an 18th-century villa, the museum was commissioned by Ernst Beyeler, Europe’s pre-eminent modern art dealer and co-founder of Art Basel, and his wife Hildy, to house their staggering collection of Monets and Mirós, Matisses and Picassos.

A long, low, temple-like shed nestled in a garden, the foundation contains within its porphyry walls a luminous sequence of galleries, with daylight flooding through slender rooftop louvers. Piano took his hi-tech fetish and wrapped it in a luxurious stone skin, foreshadowing his bigger museums to come. But it was too small right from the day it opened. Two years later, it was extended by 12 metres and soon became the most visited art museum in the country, receiving 500,000 visitors a year. The challenge was how to extend a museum already deemed perfect by its art world patrons.

“They wanted something completely different,” says Zumthor, who was selected from a shortlist of 11 architects in 2016, after 100 were approached for their ideas. “Renzo’s building is more industrial, whereas mine is almost domestic. It is the villa that this garden was missing.”

The foundation acquired the Iselin-Weber park, a formerly private woodland adjacent to the museum campus, which now doubles its size, and where Zumthor’s gallery rises like a rocky outcrop. It is one of three new structures he has designed, along with a five-storey, timber-clad office and art-handling block, and an auditorium pavilion, conceived as an open public lounge – a particularly appealing space that can be accessed without a ticket. “Ninety per cent of the time,” says the foundation’s director, Sam Keller, “museum auditoriums are dead spaces. So we’ve turned it into a social space for people to come and hang out, read books, listen to podcasts or do some work, a real extension of the park.”

The three buildings stand as an eclectic ensemble on either side of a lane, framing a public square of sorts, where a new drinking fountain trickles into a big stone trough, as in a traditional mountain village, welcoming art pilgrims to Zumthor-ville. Stone benches built into the museum facade greet weary wanderers. “A building is something you ought to be able to lean against every now and then,” says the architect, as Maurizio Cattelan’s unnerving sculpture of a drummer boy perches perilously on the parapet overhead, intermittently hammering his drum from the rooftop.

The chance for Zumthor to finally build in Basel, a few kilometres from his birthplace, clearly brought back fond memories. In a schmaltzy new two-hour documentary by Wim Wenders called From Inside Out, the misty-eyed architect explains that this “intimate building” has “a lot to do with me growing up here”. He recounts that Jura limestone was “the stone of my youth”, describing how the village fountains and the cattle troughs “all glowed”. He wanted his own building to glow, too, so he mixed Jura stone into the concrete, and had workers tamp the dry mixture by hand, laying it at a rate of no more than 45cm a day. This is all filmed with a stirring musical backdrop. He wanted the wobbly joints between each day’s work left visible, like strata of sedimentary rock.

“I call it ‘farmer concrete’,” he says. “You see it everywhere in the mountains. They make it themselves, and they don’t vibrate the mixture, so it looks rough like this. You can see the building has a history, that hands have worked on it. It’s nice if you can see those traces. If it’s too slick, you just look like a fashion magazine.”

Zumthor’s rugged brand of “rammed concrete” has become one of his highly published trademarks (and has indeed featured in fashion magazines). There is a sense of him bringing his greatest hits to the Beyeler ensemble. He used the technique for the Bruder Klaus field chapel in rural Germany and a holiday house in Devon for Alain de Botton’s Living Architecture company. The admin block, meanwhile, bears a distinct resemblance to his atelier building in Haldenstein, also in Switzerland, its elegant oak facade (masking a concrete frame) crowned with a slender corrugated canopy.

And the pavilion draws on yet another language. It’s like a warm wooden womb that’s been dug into the landscape, surrounded by walls of glass and topped with a low upholstered acoustic ceiling, full of armchairs encouraging visitors to lounge awhile. Zumthor had to wait so long for a commission in his home town, he has turned one project into three.

The galleries themselves are quite a departure from Piano’s top-lit white cubes. After the gleaming stone exterior, the interior feels almost cave-like, Monet’s waterlilies looking muddier than ever in the ground-floor gloom. Things get brighter upstairs, with large picture windows framing pastoral views in different directions as you ascend the three floors, looking towards the Black Forest on one side and the Jura mountains on the other. Limestone terrazzo floors, lime-washed walls and pale concrete ceilings create an all-encompassing world of beige, which somehow flattens the work on show, relieved only by dark timber-lined nooks for loos and lifts.

Lozenge-shaped glass lamps (“made by the only two men in Italy who have the lung capacity to do it”, I am told) provide some ambient light, while spots highlight particular works. But you might find yourself pining for the celestial top-light of Piano’s galleries next door. Despite the architect’s protestations, it oozes the aura of a luxury boutique. As one visiting Angelino noted: “It feels like a new Skims store.”

The creamy promenade culminates in a roof terrace, with more views of pretty Swiss countryside, before visitors are shuttled down a pharaonic external stairway between the concrete walls, punched with triangular openings on one side, giving glimpses of the park and a mature ginkgo tree, around which the arms of the Y-shaped building extend. Questioned about the need for all this concrete, and its attendant carbon footprint, Zumthor is adamant. “I could not make a wooden museum,” he says. “I think it is not good for art. This kind of classical art needs more substance.”
